Benchmark.title: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT
Benchmark.description: All CIS Benchmarks™ (Benchmarks) focus on technical configuration settings used to maintain and/or increase the security of the addressed technology, and they should be used in conjunction with other essential cyber hygiene tasks like: • Monitoring the base operating system and applications for vulnerabilities and quickly updating with the latest security patches. • End-point protection (Antivirus software, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), etc.). • Logging and monitoring user and system activity. In the end, the Benchmarks are designed to be a key component of a comprehensive cybersecurity program. Important Usage Information All Benchmarks are available free for non-commercial use from the CIS Website. They can be used to manually assess and remediate systems and applications. In lieu of manual assessment and remediation, there are several tools available to assist with assessment: • CIS Configuration Assessment Tool (CIS-CAT ® Pro Assessor) • CIS Benchmarks™ Certified 3rd Party Tooling These tools make the hardening process much more scalable for large numbers of systems and applications. NOTE: Some tooling focuses only on the Benchmark Recommendations that can be fully automated (skipping ones marked Manual). It is important that ALL Recommendations ( Automated and Manual) be addressed since all are important for properly securing systems and are typically in scope for audits. Key Stakeholders Cybersecurity is a collaborative effort, and cross functional cooperation is imperative within an organization to discuss, test, and deploy Benchmarks in an effective and efficient way. The Benchmarks are developed to be best practice configuration guidelines applicable to a wide range of use cases. In some organizations, exceptions to specific Recommendations will be needed, and this team should work to prioritize the problematic Recommendations based on several factors like risk, time, cost, and labor. These exceptions should be properly categorized and documented for auditing purposes. Internal Only - General Apply the Correct Version of a Benchmark Benchmarks are developed and tested for a specific set of products and versions and applying an incorrect Benchmark to a system can cause the resulting pass/fail score to be incorrect. This is due to the assessment of settings that do not apply to the target systems. To assure the correct Benchmark is being assessed: • Deploy the Benchmark applicable to the way settings are managed in the environment: An example of this is the Microsoft Windows family of Benchmarks, which have separate Benchmarks for Group Policy, Intune, and Stand-alone systems based upon how system management is deployed. Applying the wrong Benchmark in this case will give invalid results. • Use the most recent version of a Benchmark: This is true for all Benchmarks, but especially true for cloud technologies. Cloud technologies change frequently and using an older version of a Benchmark may have invalid methods for auditing and remediation. Exceptions The guidance items in the Benchmarks are called recommendations and not requirements, and exceptions to some of them are expected and acceptable. The Benchmarks strive to be a secure baseline, or starting point, for a specific technology, with known issues identified during Benchmark development are documented in the Impact section of each Recommendation. In addition, organizational, system specific requirements, or local site policy may require changes as well, or an exception to a Recommendation or group of Recommendations (e.g. A Benchmark could Recommend that a Web server not be installed on the system, but if a system's primary purpose is to function as a Webserver, there should be a documented exception to this Recommendation for that specific server). In the end, exceptions to some Benchmark Recommendations are common and acceptable, and should be handled as follows: • The reasons for the exception should be reviewed cross-functionally and be well documented for audit purposes. • A plan should be developed for mitigating, or eliminating, the exception in the future, if applicable. • If the organization decides to accept the risk of this exception (not work toward mitigation or elimination), this should be documented for audit purposes. It is the responsibility of the organization to determine their overall security policy, and which settings are applicable to their unique needs based on the overall risk profile for the organization. Internal Only - General Remediation CIS has developed Build Kits for many technologies to assist in the automation of hardening systems. Build Kits are designed to correspond to Benchmark's “Remediation” section, which provides the manual remediation steps necessary to make that Recommendation compliant to the Benchmark. When remediating systems (changing configuration settings on deployed systems as per the Benchmark's Recommendations), please approach this with caution and test thoroughly. The following is a reasonable remediation approach to follow: • CIS Build Kits, or internally developed remediation methods should never be applied to production systems without proper testing. • Proper testing consists of the following: o Understand the configuration (including installed applications) of the targeted systems. Various parts of the organization may need different configurations (e.g., software developers vs standard office workers). o Read the Impact section of the given Recommendation to help determine if there might be an issue with the targeted systems. o Test the configuration changes with representative lab system(s). If issues arise during testing, they can be resolved prior to deploying to any production systems. o When testing is complete, initially deploy to a small sub-set of production systems and monitor closely for issues. If there are issues, they can be resolved prior to deploying more broadly. o When the initial deployment above is completed successfully, iteratively deploy to additional systems and monitor closely for issues. Repeat this process until the full deployment is complete. Summary Using the Benchmarks Certified tools, working as a team with key stakeholders, being selective with exceptions, and being careful with remediation deployment, it is possible to harden large numbers of deployed systems in a cost effective, efficient, and safe manner. NOTE: As previously stated, the PDF versions of the CIS Benchmarks™ are available for free, non-commercial use on the CIS Website. All other formats of the CIS Benchmarks™ (MS Word, Excel, and Build Kits) are available for CIS SecureSuite ® members. CIS-CAT ® Pro is also available to CIS SecureSuite ® members. Internal Only - General Target Technology Details This document provides prescriptive guidance for running Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) following recommended security controls. This benchmark only includes controls which can be modified by an end user of Azure AKS and is designed to supersede all previous version of the Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark. It addresses and has been tested against Kubernetes version/s 1.29, 1.30 and 1.31. As a rule, this benchmark will address the Kubernetes versions available for cluster creation at the beginning of the consensus release period and will address Kubernetes versions that become available after that date in the next release. To obtain the latest version of this guide, please visit www.cisecurity.org. If you have questions, comments, or have identified ways to improve this guide, please write us at support@cisecurity.org.

Rule.title: Enable Diagnostic Platform Logs and Metrics
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>With Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), control plane components such as the Kubernetes API server and Kubernetes controller manager are provided as part of a managed service. You create and manage the worker nodes that run the kubelet and container runtime, and you deploy your applications through the managed Kubernetes API. To troubleshoot cluster operations and application behavior, you may need to review logs generated by these control plane components and related cluster services. To collect and analyze data from multiple sources, Azure Monitor provides a centralized monitoring platform for logs and metrics. AKS control plane logs are enabled through diagnostic settings and can be sent to a Log Analytics workspace, where they can be queried and analyzed. The workspace serves as a central repository for monitoring data and can be used alongside other Azure services such as Application Insights and Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Rationale: Exporting logs and metrics to a dedicated, persistent datastore ensures that audit data remains available in the event of a cluster security incident and provides a centralized location for analyzing log and metric data aggregated from multiple sources.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: To enable log collection for the Kubernetes master components in your AKS cluster, open the Azure portal in a web browser and complete the following steps: 1. Create or identify a Log Analytics workspace in the same subscription as the AKS cluster. 2. In the Azure portal, open your AKS cluster. 3. In the left menu, go to Monitoring, then select Diagnostic settings. 4. Select + Add diagnostic setting. 5. Enter a name such as Collect Control Plane Logs. 6. Under destination, choose Send to Log Analytics workspace and select the workspace you want to use. 7. Select the AKS log categories you want to collect. Common control plane and resource log categories include: o Kubernetes API Server o Kubernetes Audit Admin Logs o Kubernetes Controller Manager o Kubernetes Scheduler o Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler o Kubernetes Cloud Controller Manager o guard o optional: Kubernetes Audit if you need full read and write audit events o optional: CSI controller categories if they apply to your storage configuration 8. Save the diagnostic setting. 9. Wait a few minutes for logs to begin flowing into Log Analytics. 10.Verify that data is being collected by checking the workspace tables such as: o AKSControlPlane, AKSAudit, AKSAuditAdmin Recommended minimum set for most production clusters: Internal Only - General • Kubernetes API Server • Kubernetes Controller Manager • Kubernetes Scheduler • Kubernetes Cluster Autoscale • Kubernetes Cloud Controller Manager • guard • Kubernetes Audit Admin Logs NOTE: Use Kubernetes Audit only if you need a full Kubernetes API audit trail, since it can generate a much higher volume of log data.

check.check-content: AKS audit logs are not fully enabled by default when you create a cluster. What is on by default is the Azure Activity Log for Azure resource operations and AKS platform metrics. But the Kubernetes control plane/resource logs such as kube-audit, kube-audit- admin, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, and similar logs are not collected or stored until you create a diagnostic setting and route them to a destination such as Log Analytics. • If you only care about Azure-side changes like cluster creation, scaling, or configuration updates, you already have some visibility from the Activity Log by default. • If you need actual Kubernetes API audit events such as get, list, create, update, delete, patch, or post inside the cluster, you must enable diagnostic settings for AKS.

Rule.title: Ensure that the kubeconfig file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If the kubelet is configured to use a kubeconfig file, ensure that the kubelet kubeconfig file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive.
Rationale: The kubelet kubeconfig file contains the connection and authentication settings the kubelet uses to communicate with the Kubernetes API server. File permissions should be restricted to prevent unauthorized modification and to help maintain the integrity of node-to-control-plane communication. The file should be writable only by authorized administrators or system processes. The /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig is the kubelet client configuration file used by the worker node to authenticate and communicate with the Kubernetes API server.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Run the below command (based on the file location on your system) on the each worker node. For example, chmod 644 <kubeconfig file>

check.check-content: Method 1 Optional: Run the following command to enter debug mode where NODE_NAME and IMAGE are defined variables: kubectl debug node/$NODE_NAME -it --image=$IMAGE --profile=general Run the following command on each node to find the appropriate kubeconfig file: ps -efww | grep kubelet | grep -- '--kubeconfig' The command line output should show a path for kubeconfig similar to -- kubeconfig=/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig which is the location of the kubeconfig file. Run this command to obtain the kubeconfig file permissions: stat -c %a /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig (or stat -c %a /host/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig if in debub mode) The output of the above command gives you the kubeconfig file's permissions. Verify that if a file is specified and it exists, the permissions are 644 or more restrictive. Internal Only - General Method 2 Create and Run a Privileged Pod. You will need to run a pod that is privileged enough to access the host's file system. This can be achieved by deploying a pod that uses the hostPath volume to mount the node's file system into the pod. Here's an example of a simple pod definition that mounts the root of the host to /host within the pod: apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: file-check spec: volumes: - name: host-root hostPath: path: / type: Directory containers: - name: nsenter image: busybox command: ["sleep", "3600"] volumeMounts: - name: host-root mountPath: /host securityContext: privileged: true Save this to a file (e.g., file-check-pod.yaml) and create the pod: kubectl apply -f file-check-pod.yaml Once the pod is running, you can exec into it to check file permissions on the node: kubectl exec -it file-check -- sh Now you are in a shell inside the pod, but you can access the node's file system through the /host directory and check the permission level of the file: ls -l /host/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig Verify that if a file is specified and it exists, the permissions are 644 or more restrictive.

Rule.title: Ensure that the kubelet kubeconfig file ownership is set to root:root
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If kubelet is running, ensure that the ownership of the kubelet kubeconfig file is set to root:root.
Rationale: The kubelet kubeconfig file contains the connection and authentication settings used by the kubelet to communicate with the Kubernetes API server. Setting file ownership to root:root helps preserve file integrity and restrict unauthorized changes. The /var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig is the kubelet client configuration file used by the worker node to authenticate and communicate with the Kubernetes API server.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that the azure.json file has permissions set to 644 or more restrictive
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The azure.json file in an AKS worker node contains Azure cloud provider configuration used by Kubernetes and related components to interact with Azure resources such as networking, load balancing, and storage. Because this file may contain sensitive cloud configuration details, ensure that its permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive.
Rationale: The azure.json file stores Azure cloud-provider configuration used by AKS components to access Azure services such as networking, load balancing, and storage. In some AKS configurations, it can also contain service principal credentials. Restricting file permissions helps prevent unauthorized disclosure or modification of sensitive configuration and credential data. The /etc/kubernetes/azure.json is the Azure cloud-provider configuration file used for AKS integration with Azure resources.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This setting applies to the worker node kubelet and ensures that --anonymous-auth is set to false, meaning the kubelet does not accept unauthenticated anonymous requests to its HTTPS endpoint. This helps reduce the risk of unauthorized access to node-level information and operations.
Rationale: When enabled, requests that are not rejected by other configured authentication methods are treated as anonymous requests. These requests are then served by the Kubelet server. You should rely on authentication to authorize access and disallow anonymous requests. Requiring the AKS worker node kubelet --anonymous-auth setting to be false helps prevent unauthenticated access to the kubelet endpoint, reducing the risk of unauthorized disclosure of node information or misuse of kubelet functions.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: If the --anonymous-auth parameter is not set to false and manual modification is required, review the following file, which contains the KUBELET_FLAGS values used to build the kubelet command-line parameters. /etc/default/kubelet Before editing anything, enter debug mode and run chroot to verify what your node is actually using: kubectl debug node/$NODE_NAME -it --image=$IMAGE --profile=general chroot /host systemctl cat kubelet If the service shows an EnvironmentFile=/etc/default/kubelet or references KUBELET_FLAGS, that is the file you would edit. If it does not, then the next place to check is the kubelet systemd unit or drop-in, such as: /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/*.conf After a changing the kubelet config file, restart the kubelet service and check status. The usual recheck sequence would be: systemctl daemon-reload systemctl restart kubelet systemctl status kubelet -l ps -efww | grep '[k]ubelet' | grep -- '--anonymous-auth' Important: Microsoft does not recommend managing this control by manually editing node-local kubelet files and restarting kubelet. In AKS, anonymous-auth is not typically exposed through the supported kubelet customization options, and manual changes at the node level are not considered a supported or persistent method of configuration.

Rule.title: Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This worker-node kubelet setting ensures the --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow, which would permit requests to the kubelet without proper authorization checks. Using a secure mode such as Webhook helps require authorization for access to the kubelet endpoint and reduces the risk of unauthorized node-level access.
Rationale: Setting the kubelet --authorization-mode argument to a value other than AlwaysAllow helps ensure that requests to the kubelet endpoint are subject to authorization checks before access is granted. This reduces the risk of unauthorized access to node-level information and kubelet operations and supports a stronger security posture for AKS worker nodes. Using Webhook is recommended because it causes the kubelet to delegate authorization decisions to the Kubernetes API server, where access can be evaluated through centralized Kubernetes authorization controls. This provides a stronger security model than AlwaysAllow, because requests are not automatically approved and only appropriately authorized users and service accounts are permitted to access kubelet functions.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that the --client-ca-file argument is set as appropriate
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This worker-node kubelet setting ensures that the --client-ca-file argument is configured with a trusted certificate authority file so the kubelet can validate client certificates presented to its HTTPS endpoint. This helps ensure that certificate-based access to the kubelet is restricted to clients signed by an approved CA.
Rationale: The kubelet HTTPS endpoint exposes node and workload information and supports operations that can affect running pods and the worker node itself. Configuring the kubelet --client-ca-file argument causes the kubelet to trust only client certificates that can be validated against the certificate authority bundle in that file. When a client presents an X.509 certificate, the kubelet uses the CA bundle to verify that the certificate chains back to a trusted issuer before treating the request as authenticated. This helps prevent unauthorized clients from using certificate-based authentication to access kubelet functions. In practice, this strengthens node access control by ensuring that certificate-based requests to the kubelet are limited to identities issued by an approved CA rather than any arbitrary certificate source. Without an appropriate --client-ca-file value, the kubelet cannot properly validate client certificates for this authentication path, which weakens trust enforcement at the node boundary. In AKS, this remains a relevant worker-node hardening control and is reflected in Microsoft’s AKS CIS guidance for kubelet configuration.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that the --read-only-port is set to 0
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>this worker-node kubelet setting ensures that the --read-only-port value is set to 0, which disables the kubelet’s unauthenticated read-only endpoint. This helps prevent unauthenticated access to node and workload information exposed by the kubelet and remains a current AKS worker-node control.
Rationale: The kubelet read-only port exposes a read-only HTTP endpoint on the worker node that does not enforce authentication or authorization. In current Kubernetes configuration, readOnlyPort set to 0 disables that service, while any nonzero value enables an endpoint that can expose node and workload information without the normal kubelet access controls. For AKS worker nodes, setting --read-only-port to 0 helps remove an unnecessary unauthenticated interface from the node and reduces the risk of information disclosure through the kubelet. From a hardening perspective, the kubelet should expose management functionality only through its secured interfaces, where authentication and authorization controls can be applied. Leaving the read-only port enabled creates an alternate access path that bypasses those protections and can provide visibility into node and pod state that should be restricted to authorized clients.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that the --make-iptables-util-chains argument is set to true
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The --make-iptables-util-chains setting ensures the kubelet creates the iptables utility hint chain used by other components to identify the node’s iptables configuration. This is important because it helps maintain predictable networking behavior on the worker node and supports components that rely on that hint to determine how iptables is configured on the host. In practice, AKS nodes often rely on the kubelet default value of true, so the setting may not always appear explicitly in a node-local file even though the intended behavior is still in effect.
Rationale: In AKS, setting --make-iptables-util-chains to true ensures the worker-node kubelet creates the KUBE-IPTABLES-HINT chain on the host. Kubernetes documents this setting with a default of true, and the purpose of the hint chain is to let other components detect the node’s iptables configuration and behave consistently. In AKS, that matters because worker-node networking depends on predictable host networking behavior, and this setting helps preserve the kubelet’s expected iptables utility-chain behavior on the node. If this value were set to false, the kubelet would stop creating that hint chain. In AKS, that could make node-level networking behavior less predictable for components or tooling that rely on the presence of KUBE-IPTABLES-HINT to understand the host’s iptables environment. AKS guidance still treats this as a current worker-node setting, so keeping it at true aligns with both the kubelet’s intended default behavior and AKS’s expected node hardening posture.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that the kubelet eventRecordQPS setting is configured to a level that ensures appropriate event capture.
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In AKS, eventRecordQPS is the worker-node kubelet setting that controls the maximum rate at which the kubelet can create Kubernetes events. These events provide operational visibility into node and pod activity, and the setting helps determine whether the kubelet records that activity at a rate that matches the workload running on the node. An appropriate value is one that supports expected event volume without excessive throttling; the current kubelet configuration API defines a default of 50, and a value of 0 means no rate limit is enforced. AKS continues to treat this as a worker-node setting that should be configured to support appropriate event capture.
Rationale: In AKS, eventRecordQPS matters because it controls how quickly the worker-node kubelet can create Kubernetes events, which are a key source of operational visibility for node and pod activity. If the value is set too low, the kubelet can throttle event creation during bursts of activity, which can reduce visibility into restarts, health changes, image pull failures, and other important state transitions. The current kubelet configuration API defines a default of 50, and 0 means no rate limit is enforced. eventBurst works with this setting to allow short bursts above the steady-state rate, with a default of 100. As technical background, --event-qps is the older command-line alternative to eventRecordQPS and may still be used in the latest AKS configuration. Kubernetes still documents -event-qps, but marks it as deprecated in favor of the kubelet configuration file. It is also important not to treat the two forms identically: eventRecordQPS: 0 means unlimited event creation, while --event-qps=0 falls back to a default QPS of 5. For current AKS-focused documentation, eventRecordQPS should be treated as the primary setting, with --event-qps referenced only as a legacy equivalent.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure that rotateCertificates is set to true
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The value of rotateCertificates ( -rotate-certificates argument) should be set to true because it allows the kubelet to automatically generate a new key and request a replacement client certificate from the Kubernetes API as the current certificate approaches expiration. That client certificate is what the kubelet uses to authenticate to the API server, so keeping rotation enabled helps prevent the node from relying on an aging certificate that could eventually become stale or expire. In practical terms, the expected secure state is that certificate rotation is on, which in AKS aligns with the CIS control that the --rotate-certificates argument must not be set to false.
Rationale: This setting should be true because it verifies that kubelet identity is being refreshed through Kubernetes’ normal PKI renewal process rather than depending on a long-lived credential. From a security and operational control standpoint, that matters because static node credentials are harder to govern over time and provide less assurance that node authentication is being actively maintained through the platform’s intended certificate workflow. The related RotateKubeletServerCertificate setting should be evaluated separately because it covers a different certificate role. rotateCertificates governs the kubelet’s outbound client identity to the control plane, while RotateKubeletServerCertificate is tied to kubelet serving certificate rotation, used when the kubelet presents a TLS certificate as a server endpoint. Kubernetes documents serving certificate rotation through TLS bootstrapping and notes that serverTLSBootstrap depends on the RotateKubeletServerCertificate feature, and AKS lists the two controls separately in its CIS mapping. Together, they show whether both sides of kubelet certificate trust are being managed correctly, not just one.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: If an audit shows rotateCertificates set to false or blank, the preferred remediation is to replace the affected node pool with a new pool and let the kubelet come up through the normal AKS node-pool configuration path, rather than trying to force a one-off manual change onto existing nodes. This is the preferred approach because the setting affects kubelet client certificate rotation, which is part of how each node maintains authenticated trust with the Kubernetes API server over time. Rebuilding the pool allows new nodes to be provisioned, bootstrapped, and joined through the same managed configuration path, which helps ensure consistent kubelet behavior across the pool and avoids carrying forward nodes whose certificate lifecycle or startup arguments may already have drifted from the intended state. The rebuilding the node pool supports durability and consistency: • AKS applies kubelet tuning through node-pool configuration rather than through ad hoc per-node changes. • A manual edit to /etc/default/kubelet does not work well because it changes only the local VM, can be overwritten during reprovisioning or image refresh, and can leave nodes in the same pool running with different kubelet behavior. Internal Only - General • Because rotateCertificates is not handled as a normal AKS-exposed node- pool setting, az aks nodepool update is not a dependable way to remediate this finding. • Replacing the node pool helps ensure the kubelet starts through a repeatable, pool-level configuration path instead of relying on one-off node changes that may not remain consistent across the environment. Important: Editing /etc/default/kubelet is not recommended, even if it appears to work, because that file feeds KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS, which acts as a last-resort override with higher priority than conflicting kubelet configuration. That makes the change node-local hard to govern, can mask the intended kubelet config, and can create configuration drift between nodes in the same pool. In AKS, that risk is even greater because normal lifecycle events such as scale-out, upgrade, or reimage can replace the VM and remove reliance on the original hand-edited state.

Rule.title: Ensure that the RotateKubeletServerCertificate argument is set to true
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The RotateKubeletServerCertificate argument is a control that corresponds to kubelet serving certificate rotation. In practical terms, it means the kubelet uses server TLS bootstrapping to obtain and rotate a serving certificate signed by the cluster CA for the kubelet’s own HTTPS endpoint, rather than relying on a locally self-signed serving certificate. AKS treats this as a valid CIS-aligned control and documents kubelet serving certificate rotation separately from other certificate features.
Rationale: This setting covers a different trust boundary than rotateCertificates. The rotateCertificates setting governs the kubelet’s client certificate, which the node uses to authenticate to the API server, while RotateKubeletServerCertificate governs the kubelet’s server-side TLS identity, which is what other components see when they connect to the kubelet’s HTTPS endpoint. Reviewing only the client-side control can leave a gap: node authentication to the control plane may be healthy while the kubelet’s serving endpoint is still operating with a weaker or less-governed certificate model.</VulnDiscussion>

In addition, replacing the node pool gives you a consistent, repeatable way to bring every node up through the same managed certificate path. Rule.title: Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Verify that cluster-admin access in AKS is granted only to identities with a documented need for full cluster-wide administration. In AKS, this review should cover both Kubernetes-native privilege paths, such as ClusterRoleBinding assignments to the cluster-admin ClusterRole, and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization assignments, such as Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin, because AKS supports authorization through both models depending on the identity and access path. Where administrative needs are limited to a namespace, application, or team boundary, lower-privilege roles and namespace-scoped bindings should be used instead of cluster-wide administrative access.
Rationale: This control supports least privilege in the highest-risk portion of the AKS authorization model. Microsoft’s AKS guidance emphasizes granular role assignment for Kubernetes API access, and AKS provides built-in Reader, Writer, Admin, and Cluster Admin roles specifically so permissions can be scoped to operational need rather than defaulting to full-cluster authority. Kubernetes guidance reinforces the same principle by recommending minimal RBAC rights for users and service accounts, favoring namespace-level permissions where possible and warning against unrestricted privilege constructs. Excessive RBAC privileges in Kubernetes can create direct or indirect escalation paths. AKS documentation explicitly notes, for example, that even read access to Secrets can expose service account credentials and enable API access as that service account within the namespace, while Kubernetes documents broader escalation risks around powerful permissions and cluster-scoped bindings. Because AKS may authorize Microsoft Entra identities through Azure RBAC while service accounts continue to rely on Kubernetes RBAC, controlling cluster-admin use is necessary to keep privileged access exceptional, auditable, and bounded.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Verify that access to Kubernetes Secret objects in AKS are granted to only identities with a defined purpose. The review should include Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization assignments, Kubernetes RBAC roles and bindings, and service account permissions, with particular attention to permissions that allow get, list, or watch access to secrets, because those permissions expose sensitive namespace-scoped data. In AKS, access should be limited to the minimum scope and privilege necessary for the workload or administrator function being performed. The Kubernetes API stores secrets, which may be service account tokens for the Kubernetes API or credentials used by workloads in the cluster. Access to these secrets should be restricted to the smallest possible group of users to reduce the risk of privilege escalation.
Rationale: This requirement is necessary because unnecessary access to Secrets in AKS increases the risk of credential exposure and privilege escalation. Microsoft’s AKS guidance notes that access to secret contents can expose service account credentials, and that combining secret access with the ability to run pods as service accounts can enable a principal to gain that service account’s API access level. Kubernetes also treats get, list, and watch access to Secret objects as sensitive because those permissions can reveal secret contents directly or indirectly. Minimizing secret access in AKS therefore helps reduce the likelihood that a user, workload, or service account can expose sensitive data or expand its effective privileges beyond what is required.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Verify that Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole definitions in AKS do not use wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups unless a documented administrative need exists. The audit should include any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding that assigns those roles to users, groups, or service accounts, because in Kubernetes RBAC a role defines additive permissions and bindings determine which principals receive them. In AKS, this is particularly relevant for service accounts because their authorization continues to rely on Kubernetes RBAC.
Rationale: This recommendation is necessary because wildcard permissions make RBAC scope harder to predict and harder to constrain. Kubernetes guidance explicitly recommends avoiding wildcard permissions where possible, especially across all resources, because Kubernetes is extensible and wildcard access applies not only to resource types that exist today but also to resource types introduced later. Since RBAC permissions are purely additive, a wildcard can silently expand what a bound principal is allowed to do without any corresponding narrowing control in the role itself. In AKS, that risk remains material even when Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization is enabled, because AKS states that identities outside Microsoft Entra ID, including Kubernetes service accounts, fall back to normal Kubernetes RBAC authorization. As a result, wildcard rules in Role and ClusterRole objects can still overprivilege workloads and controllers that run under service accounts, even in clusters where human user access is otherwise managed through Azure RBAC.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Minimize access to create pods
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The ability to create pods in a namespace can provide a number of opportunities for privilege escalation, such as assigning privileged service accounts to these pods or mounting hostPaths with access to sensitive data (unless Pod Security Policies are implemented to restrict this access) This verifies that permission to create or run pods in AKS is granted only to identities with a documented operational need. The review should include RBAC assignments to users, groups, and service accounts that allow pod creation or the ability to run pods under service accounts, because AKS treats pod execution as a security-relevant action rather than a routine read/write permission. As such, access to create new pods should be restricted to the smallest possible group of users.
Rationale: This requirement is necessary because pod creation in AKS can translate into API access through service accounts. Microsoft’s AKS identity guidance states that service account credentials are stored as Kubernetes secrets and used by authorized pods to communicate with the API server, and AKS RBAC guidance notes that the ability to run pods as any service account in a namespace can be used to gain that service account’s API access level. The ability to create pods in a cluster opens up possibilities for privilege escalation and should be restricted, where possible.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: The following steps help reduce pod-creation access to the minimum required in AKS • Identify all Azure RBAC assignments and Kubernetes RBAC bindings that allow pod creation in AKS, including namespace-scoped and cluster-scoped access. • Remove pod-creation rights from any user, group, or service account that does not have a documented operational need. • Replace broad permissions with the lowest-privilege role and narrowest scope necessary, preferably at the namespace level rather than cluster-wide. • Ensure workloads use dedicated service accounts with only the permissions required for that application or controller. • Revalidate access after changes to confirm required workloads still run and that unnecessary pod-creation rights have been removed.

check.check-content: Review AKS authorization to determine whether access is controlled through Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, Kubernetes RBAC, or both, then identify the users, groups, and service accounts that can create pods. Validate whether each assignment is required for each role, with particular attention to service accounts and namespace write access, because Microsoft notes that the ability to run pods as a service account can be used to gain that service account’s API access level. Any excessive pod- creation rights should be flagged for remediation and reduced to a lower-privilege role or narrower scope.

Rule.title: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used by verifying that application and automation pods in AKS do not rely on the namespace default service account when a dedicated service account should be used instead. Confirm that workloads explicitly specify the intended serviceAccountName, the default service account is not bound to unnecessary Kubernetes RBAC permissions, and it is not being used as the identity boundary for workloads that need distinct API permissions or Microsoft Entra Workload ID behavior.
Rationale: This is recommended because AKS service accounts are operational identities, not just deployment defaults. Microsoft states that service account credentials are stored as Kubernetes secrets and are used by authorized pods to communicate with the Kubernetes API server. AKS also documents that when Azure RBAC integration is used, identities outside Microsoft Entra ID, including Kubernetes service accounts, still fall back to normal Kubernetes RBAC. Using the default service account therefore makes it harder to apply least privilege cleanly, because multiple workloads can end up sharing the same Kubernetes identity and API authorization path within a namespace. AKS documentation also shows that service-account token handling is security-relevant: Microsoft publishes an AKS Azure Policy built-in that sets automountServiceAccountToken to false because avoiding default token auto- mounting increases security, and AKS Workload ID uses explicit pod labels plus service-account configuration to project and exchange service-account tokens for Microsoft Entra access tokens. Together, that guidance supports using dedicated, intentional service accounts rather than actively relying on the default account for ordinary workloads.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Apply the following steps to replace default service-account usage with dedicated, least- privileged workload identities in AKS: • Update workloads to explicitly set a dedicated serviceAccountName instead of inheriting the namespace default service account. • Remove unnecessary RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments from the default service account, and keep any remaining access minimal and namespace-scoped. • Set automountServiceAccountToken to false where Kubernetes API access is not required to prevent default token auto-mounting. • Review both the ServiceAccount and Pod settings for automountServiceAccountToken, and treat the Pod value as authoritative when both are defined. • For workloads that need Azure resource access, use Microsoft Entra Workload ID with explicit workload configuration instead of the namespace default service account.

check.check-content: Review pods in all AKS namespaces to identify workloads that do not explicitly set serviceAccountName and therefore use the namespace default service account. Then review RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments for each default service account to confirm it is not granted unnecessary permissions, since AKS states that service account credentials are used by authorized pods to communicate with the API server and that service accounts continue to rely on Kubernetes RBAC. In addition, verify whether service account tokens are being mounted unnecessarily by checking the automountServiceAccountToken setting at the pod and service account level. Microsoft’s AKS policy guidance states that setting automountServiceAccountToken to false increases security by avoiding default token auto-mounting, so any workload using the default service account or auto- mounting a token without a documented need should be flagged for remediation. Review the automountServiceAccountToken setting on both the Pod and its associated ServiceAccount, and treat the Pod setting as authoritative where both are defined. kubectl get serviceaccount $SERVICE_ACCOUNT -n $NAMESPACE -o yaml kubectl get pod $POD_NAME -n $NAMESPACE -o yaml

Rule.title: Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Review that service account tokens in AKS are mounted only for pods that require Kubernetes API access or an explicitly configured workload identity flow. Confirm that pods and service accounts are not broadly relying on default token mounting, and that token projection is limited to workloads with a defined operational need. AKS reflects this through a built-in policy that sets automountServiceAccountToken to false, and through workload identity guidance that requires explicit pod labeling for token projection.
Rationale: Limiting service account token mounts is important because a mounted token is an authentication credential. AKS states that service account credentials are stored as Kubernetes secrets and are used by authorized pods to communicate with the Kubernetes API server, and AKS policy guidance states that setting automountServiceAccountToken to false increases security by avoiding default token auto-mounting. AKS workload identity guidance reinforces the same principle by making projected service-account tokens explicit rather than automatic. Microsoft documents that pods must be labeled azure.workload.identity/use: "true" for AKS workload identity behavior, which supports treating token mounting as an intentional workload requirement rather than a default behavior.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Apply the following steps to reduce unnecessary service account token mounting in AKS: • Set automountServiceAccountToken to false for pods and service accounts that do not require Kubernetes API access. AKS policy guidance states that this increases security by avoiding default token auto-mounting. • Update workloads to use a dedicated serviceAccountName only where a service account token is operationally required, instead of inheriting token behavior from the namespace default service account. AKS states that service account credentials are used by authorized pods to communicate with the API server. • For workloads that need Azure resource access, use Microsoft Entra Workload ID with explicit workload configuration rather than broad default token mounting. AKS documents that workload identity token projection is enabled only for explicitly configured pods. • Revalidate workloads after the change to confirm that only pods with a documented need continue to receive service account tokens.

check.check-content: Review pods and service accounts in each AKS namespace to confirm service account tokens are mounted only where Kubernetes API access or workload identity is required. Check automountServiceAccountToken at both the Pod and ServiceAccount level, and flag workloads that receive tokens without a documented need. Microsoft’s AKS policy guidance states that setting automountServiceAccountToken to false increases security by avoiding default auto-mounting, and Kubernetes documents that the Pod value takes precedence if both the Pod and ServiceAccount specify it. Review the automountServiceAccountToken setting on both the Pod and its associated ServiceAccount, and treat the Pod setting as authoritative where both are defined. kubectl get serviceaccount $SERVICE_ACCOUNT -n $NAMESPACE -o yaml kubectl get pod $POD_NAME -n $NAMESPACE -o yaml

Rule.title: Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Cluster roles and roles with the impersonate, bind or escalate permissions should not be granted unless strictly required. Each of these permissions allow a particular subject to escalate their privileges beyond those explicitly granted by cluster administrators Review AKS authorization assignments to ensure bind, escalate, and impersonation permissions are granted only to identities with a documented administrative need. This review should cover Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole design, RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments, and any Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization custom roles that include AKS managed-cluster actions such as .../roles/bind/action,.../clusterroles/escalate/action, or .../serviceaccounts/impersonate/action.
Rationale: These permissions are high risk because they affect the authorization model itself, not just routine resource access. In AKS, Microsoft defines actions to bind roles, escalate roles, and impersonate users, groups, and service accounts. It is AKS best-practice to assign the least amount of permission required to those capabilities so they remain tightly restricted. The impersonate privilege allows a subject to impersonate other users gaining their rights to the cluster. The bind privilege allows the subject to add a binding to a cluster role or role which escalates their effective permissions in the cluster. The escalate privilege allows a subject to modify cluster roles to which they are bound, increasing their rights to that level. Each of these permissions has the potential to allow for privilege escalation to cluster-admin level.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Remove bind, escalate, and impersonation permissions from any custom Role or ClusterRole that does not require them for an approved administrative function. Where these permissions are required, keep them limited to the smallest practical scope and avoid assigning them to workload service accounts, since AKS recommends minimum required permissions and service accounts continue to rely on Kubernetes RBAC. • Update each affected custom Role to remove unnecessary bind, escalate, or impersonat e rules. • Update each affected custom ClusterRole to retain only the specific elevated permission that is explicitly required. • Replace broad assignments with lower-privilege roles and reduce scope from cluster-wide to namespace-scoped where possible. • Do not assign these permissions to workload service accounts unless there is a documented and approved need. • Revalidate access after the change to confirm that only approved administrative identities retain these permissions. Internal Only - General

check.check-content: Review AKS RBAC to identify any users, groups, or service accounts granted bind, escalate, or impersonation permissions through Kubernetes RBAC or Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. • Identify roles and bindings that include bind, escalate, or impersonation permissions. • Determine which users, groups, or service accounts receive those permissions. • Validate that each assignment is required for a defined administrative function. • Flag any cluster-scoped or service-account assignment that lacks a documented need. Use the following commands to identify custom Kubernetes RBAC roles in the AKS cluster that include the sensitive bind, escalate, or impersonate permissions. The first command reviews all namespace-scoped custom Role objects for these permissions. The second command reviews only custom ClusterRole objects and excludes the default delivered Kubernetes roles, helping focus the audit on non-default RBAC definitions that may introduce elevated privilege paths. kubectl get roles -A -o yaml | grep -nE 'bind|escalate|impersonate' kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r ' .items[] | select(.metadata.labels["kubernetes.io/bootstrapping"] != "rbac- defaults") | select(any(.rules[]?; any(.verbs[]?; .=="bind" or .=="escalate" or .=="impersonate"))) | .metadata.name '

Rule.title: Minimize access to create persistent volumes
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Permission to create persistent storage in AKS is granted only where it is required. In AKS, this includes direct creation of PersistentVolume objects and, more commonly, the ability to trigger dynamic provisioning through PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass use, because AKS storage classes and CSI drivers can create the underlying Azure Disk, Azure File share, or other backed storage on demand. For service accounts, this remains an RBAC concern because AKS uses Kubernetes RBAC to grant access to Kubernetes resources, and requests from identities outside Microsoft Entra ID, including Kubernetes service accounts, continue to defer to normal Kubernetes RBAC.
Rationale: Minimizing this access is important because persistent volumes in AKS are durable resources that can outlive individual pods, and dynamic provisioning can automatically create backing Azure storage when a claim is submitted. Microsoft’s AKS storage guidance states that a PV can exist beyond the lifetime of a pod, that dynamic provisioning uses a storage class to determine what resource to create, and that the Azure Disk and Azure Files CSI drivers manage the lifecycle of those Azure storage resources. As a result, storage-creation rights are more sensitive than ordinary workload write access: they can allocate long-lived storage, influence performance tier and storage type, and establish new data persistence paths inside the cluster.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Remove persistent-storage creation rights from any user, group, or service account that does not require them, and replace broad assignments with the lowest-privilege role and narrowest scope possible. Limit direct PersistentVolume and StorageClass administration to approved administrators, and allow workloads to use only the PersistentVolumeClaim access they need for approved storage classes. After changes are made, verify that required applications can still provision storage through the intended AKS CSI driver path. Where possible, remove create access to PersistentVolume objects in the cluster.

check.check-content: Review AKS RBAC to identify any users, groups, or service accounts that can create PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, or StorageClass resources. In AKS, this review should include PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass permissions because persistent storage is commonly provisioned dynamically through CSI drivers rather than by manually creating PersistentVolume objects.

Rule.title: Minimize access to the proxy sub-resource of nodes
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Review AKS RBAC to ensure access to the nodes/proxy subresource is granted only to identities with a documented operational need. This review should include Role and ClusterRole rules, RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments, and any service accounts that receive node-proxy access, because AKS uses Kubernetes RBAC to grant in-cluster permissions and service accounts continue to rely on Kubernetes RBAC authorization. Microsoft’s AKS guidance also indicates that nodes/proxy is a privileged access path by explicitly denying workloads that grant nodes/proxy permissions on managed system node pools except for approved system users and groups. Users with access to the Proxy sub-resource of Node objects automatically have permissions to use the kubelet API, which may allow for privilege escalation or bypass cluster security controls such as audit logs. Direct access to the kubelet API bypasses controls like audit logging (there is no audit log of kubelet API access) and admission control.
Rationale: Limiting nodes/proxy access is important because AKS treats node access as a privileged operation rather than ordinary workload access. Microsoft’s node-access guidance says direct access to AKS nodes is used for maintenance, log collection, or troubleshooting, and that nodes aren’t exposed to the internet; instead, access is expected through controlled methods such as kubectl debug or the node’s private IP. AKS Automatic reinforces the same principle by blocking workloads that grant nodes/proxy permissions on managed system node pools unless they are approved system identities.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Reduce custom RBAC access to the nodes/proxy API path so it is limited to approved administrative identities that require node-level access. In AKS, node access is treated as privileged, and service accounts continue to use Kubernetes RBAC for in-cluster authorization. Internal Only - General • Remove nodes/proxy from any custom Role or ClusterRole where node-level proxying is not explicitly required for support, troubleshooting, or platform operations. • Where some node-related access is still needed, replace nodes/proxy with narrower permissions on only the specific resources and verbs required, and reduce scope from ClusterRole to namespace-scoped Role where the function allows it. AKS guidance favors minimum required permissions and separation of access boundaries. • Remove any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding that grants nodes/proxy to workload service accounts, CI/CD identities, or broad operator groups unless there is an approved exception tied to a defined operational function. • For approved administrative use cases, keep nodes/proxy assigned only to dedicated support or platform-admin identities, and document the purpose, scope, and owner of each remaining assignment. • Revalidate the updated roles and bindings after the change to confirm that required node-support tasks still work and that no unnecessary custom RBAC objects retain nodes/proxy access.

check.check-content: Review AKS RBAC to identify custom Role and ClusterRole objects that grant access to the nodes/proxy subresource, and validate that each permission is required for an approved troubleshooting, maintenance, or platform-administration function. This review should focus on customer-managed RBAC because AKS uses Kubernetes RBAC to grant in-cluster permissions, and service accounts continue to rely on Kubernetes RBAC authorization when the identity is outside Microsoft Entra ID. The command below returns only roles whose actual RBAC rules include nodes/proxy, and it filters out Kubernetes default bootstrapped roles plus system: -prefixed roles so the output is more focused on custom RBAC rather than delivered platform roles. This command returns each custom Role or ClusterRole whose RBAC rules include nodes/proxy, along with the namespace, role name, and allowed verbs. It is intended to give a cleaner view of customer-managed node-proxy access by excluding default bootstrapped roles and system:-prefixed roles, so you can focus the audit on custom RBAC assignments that may require review. kubectl get roles,clusterroles -A -o json | jq -r ' .items[] | select(any(.rules[]?; any(.resources[]?; .=="nodes/proxy"))) | select( (.kind=="Role") or ( .kind=="ClusterRole" and (.metadata.labels["kubernetes.io/bootstrapping"] != "rbac- defaults") and (.metadata.name | startswith("system:") | not) ) ) | [ .kind, (.metadata.namespace // "-"), .metadata.name, ( [.rules[]? | select(any(.resources[]?; .=="nodes/proxy")) | "verbs=" + ((.verbs // []) | join(",")) ] | join("; ") ) ] | @tsv '

Rule.title: Minimize access to the approval sub-resource of CertificateSigningRequests objects
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize access to the approval sub-resource of CertificateSigningRequests objects so that only tightly controlled administrative identities can approve certificate requests in AKS. AKS uses certificates for component authentication, and each kubelet creates a CSR for communication to the API server that is signed by the cluster CA at the same time, AKS authorization is intentionally granular and is meant to give users, groups, and service accounts access only to the resources they require. In practice, this means CSR approval authority should not be broadly included in general-purpose cluster roles, namespace admin roles, or workload identities. Users with access to the update the approval sub-resource of CertificateSigningRequests objects can approve new client certificates for the Kubernetes API effectively allowing them to create new high-privileged user accounts. This can allow for privilege escalation to full cluster administrator, depending on users configured in the cluster
Rationale: it is important to preserve the integrity of the AKS trust chain and keep certificate issuance under strict administrative control. Microsoft recommends securing API server access with the lowest possible permission levels, and AKS RBAC is designed to scope permissions precisely across cluster and namespace boundaries. Because AKS continues to use service accounts and projected service account tokens as part of its identity model, any unnecessary expansion of privileged API permissions increases the chance that a compromised user, pod, or service account could participate in higher- trust authentication flows than intended. Limiting CSR approval helps keep certificate- based trust separate from ordinary workload and namespace operations.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Remediate this control by removing certificatesigningrequests/approval access from any Role or ClusterRole that is not explicitly required for cluster-level certificate administration, then rebind that capability only to tightly controlled AKS administrative identities. In AKS, the preferred model is to use Microsoft Entra integration with least- privilege Kubernetes RBAC and, where enabled, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, while keeping cluster-wide permissions narrowly scoped. The remediation should also account for service-account exposure, because Microsoft documents that access to Secrets or the ability to run pods as any service account can become a privilege-escalation path to Kubernetes API access. Finally, validate that only expected AKS certificate workflows, such as kubelet TLS bootstrapping and rotation, continue to generate approved CSRs after permissions are tightened.

check.check-content: Audit this control by reviewing how privileged access is actually granted across the AKS authorization model and then verifying that CSR approval authority is limited to a very small set of approved administrative identities. In AKS, this is not a discrete platform setting it is a least-privilege review across Microsoft Entra-integrated access, Kubernetes RBAC, and, where enabled, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. The review should confirm whether any role can approve the CertificateSigningRequests approval subresource, whether that privilege is inherited by users, groups, or service accounts that do not require it, and whether observed CSR activity matches normal AKS certificate workflows such as kubelet TLS bootstrapping and certificate rotation. • Determine whether access is governed by Kubernetes RBAC, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, or both. • Review Role and ClusterRole rules for the certificatesigningrequests/approval subresource. • Trace any matching rules through RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments to the exact users, groups, and service accounts that receive them. • Confirm the permission is restricted to tightly controlled cluster-admin identities and not exposed through broad custom roles or workload identities.

Rule.title: Minimize access to webhook configuration objects
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize access to webhook configuration objects so that only tightly controlled cluster- administrative identities can create, update, or delete ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration resources in AKS. Admission controllers run after authentication and authorization but before an object is persisted, and Microsoft’s AKS documentation shows that webhook configurations define the webhook service endpoint and related trust material used by the API server. In AKS, these objects can govern validation and mutation behavior used by components such as Azure Policy / Gatekeeper, service-mesh injectors, and other admission integrations, so they should not be broadly writable by general users, namespace operators, or workload service accounts. Users with rights to create/modify/delete validatingwebhookconfigurations or mutatingwebhookconfigurations can control webhooks that can read any object admitted to the cluster, and in the case of mutating webhooks, also mutate admitted objects. This could allow for privilege escalation or disruption of the operation of the cluster.
Rationale: Preserve the integrity of the AKS admission path and prevent non-administrative identities from changing how the API server evaluates or mutates requests. Microsoft’s AKS identity guidance states that Kubernetes RBAC should grant users, groups, and service accounts only the resources they need, and that service accounts continue to rely on normal Kubernetes RBAC even when Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization is enabled for Microsoft Entra identities. Because webhook configuration objects determine which requests are intercepted and which in-cluster service receives those admission callbacks, broad write access creates a privilege boundary issue: a compromised user or service account with webhook- configuration permissions could alter policy-enforcement behavior or redirect admission processing in ways that exceed its intended operational role. Internal Only - General</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Remediate this control by removing permission to create, update, patch, or delete ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects from broad ClusterRole and Role assignments, and then rebinding that access only to tightly controlled cluster-administrative identities. In AKS, this should be implemented through least-privilege Kubernetes RBAC and, where used, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, with access granted through centrally managed identity groups rather than widely distributed individual assignments. Internal Only - General Service-account permissions should be reviewed as part of the same effort so workload identities do not inherit cluster-scoped webhook-management capability. Review each webhook configuration and narrow its match criteria to only the required namespaces, resources, and operations. In AKS, Microsoft recommends avoiding broad webhook scope, excluding AKS internal namespaces and managed resources, and ensuring webhook backends remain healthy so admission processing does not disrupt API- server requests or normal cluster lifecycle operations.

check.check-content: Audit this control by identifying who can modify cluster-scoped webhook configuration resources and confirming that webhook definitions are limited to approved admission use cases in AKS. The review should verify that ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects are present only where operationally required, that their scope is not broader than necessary, and that access to manage them is restricted through least-privilege RBAC. Microsoft’s AKS guidance also warns that misconfigured admission webhooks can disrupt cluster operations, especially when they apply too broadly or affect AKS-managed resources. • Identify whether cluster access is governed through Kubernetes RBAC alone or also through Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. • Review cluster-scoped roles for permissions on validatingwebhookconfigurations and mutatingwebhookconfigurations. • Trace those permissions through bindings to the exact users, groups, and service accounts that receive them. • Review existing webhook configurations to confirm their rules, selectors, and scope are narrowly defined and do not target AKS-managed namespaces or resources. kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o wide This command retrieves all validating and mutating admission webhook configuration objects in the cluster and displays them in an expanded view so they can be reviewed for presence, scope, and expected use.

Rule.title: Minimize access to the service account token creation
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize access to service account token creation so that only tightly controlled administrative or platform identities can request tokens for Kubernetes service accounts in AKS. AKS uses service accounts as a core Kubernetes identity type and documents that workloads can use Service Account Token Volume Projection to obtain a Kubernetes token, and AKS OIDC guidance states that projected service account tokens are required for Kubernetes 1.30+ clusters, with a maximum token lifetime of 24 hours. In practice, permission to create or issue these tokens should not be broadly granted to namespace operators, CI/CD identities, or general workload service accounts. Users with rights to create new service account tokens at a cluster level, can create long-lived privileged credentials in the cluster. This could allow for privilege escalation and persistent access to the cluster, even if the users account has been revoked.
Rationale: Microsoft’s AKS guidance states that Kubernetes RBAC should grant users, groups, and service accounts only the resources they need, and Microsoft also notes that Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization and Kubernetes RBAC must still be managed separately. In addition, AKS built-in role guidance warns that access patterns involving Secrets or the ability to run pods as any service account can be used to gain that service account’s API access. By extension, granting token-creation capability would provide an even more direct path to usable service-account credentials. The last sentence is an inference from Microsoft’s documented credential model and privilege- escalation guidance.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Review all Role and ClusterRole definitions for access to the serviceaccounts/token subresource, removing that permission from any user, group, CI/CD identity, or workload service account that does not have a documented operational requirement. In AKS, service accounts are still governed through Kubernetes RBAC, and Microsoft’s guidance is to grant users, groups, and service accounts only the permissions they need. This review should also account for Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization where it is enabled, because Microsoft documents that Microsoft Entra identities and Kubernetes service accounts follow different authorization paths in AKS. 1. Review Role and ClusterRole objects for serviceaccounts/token access. 2. Remove that permission from broad operational roles, CI/CD identities, and workload service accounts. 3. Reassign it only to approved administrative or platform identities with a documented need. 4. Validate that required workload identity and projected-token flows still function correctly. Internal Only - General 5. Recheck bindings to confirm no unintended subject still inherits token-creation rights

check.check-content: Confirm that the ability to create service account tokens is restricted to only the identities that explicitly require it for approved platform or workload operations. In AKS, service accounts remain Kubernetes identities governed by Kubernetes RBAC, while Microsoft Entra Workload ID relies on projected service account tokens and OIDC federation to obtain Azure access tokens, so unnecessary token-creation rights should be treated as a credential-issuance risk rather than a routine namespace permission. Where Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization is enabled, review it alongside Kubernetes RBAC because the two authorization models are managed separately in AKS. • Determine whether the cluster uses Kubernetes RBAC only or Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization in addition to Kubernetes RBAC. • Review cluster and namespace roles for permission to create the serviceaccounts/token subresource or other paths that can issue service account credentials. • Trace those permissions through bindings to the exact users, groups, and service accounts that inherit them. • Confirm each assignee has a documented need for token issuance and that the permission is not exposed through broad custom roles, CI/CD identities, or workload service accounts. • Validate that current service-account token use aligns with expected AKS workload identity or platform behavior and not ad hoc credential minting. Review the users who have access to create the token sub-resource of serviceaccount objects in the Kubernetes API.

Rule.title: Minimize the admission of privileged containers
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize the admission of privileged containers by restricting the ability to create pods whose containers, init containers, or ephemeral containers run with securityContext.privileged=true, and reserve that capability for narrowly approved platform scenarios only. In AKS, this remains applicable because privileged workload admission can be governed at namespace scope with Pod Security Admission and at cluster scope with Azure Policy or Deployment Safeguards, which Microsoft documents as supported enforcement paths for secure workload admission. Do not generally permit containers to be run with the securityContext.privileged flag set to true.
Rationale: Privileged containers have access to all Linux Kernel capabilities and devices. A container running with full privileges can do almost everything that the host can do. This flag exists to allow special use-cases, like manipulating the network stack and accessing devices. There should be at least one admission control policy defined which does not permit privileged containers. If you need to run privileged containers, this should be defined in a separate policy and you should carefully check to ensure that only limited service accounts and users are given permission to use that policy.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Add policies to each namespace in the cluster which has user workloads to restrict the admission of privileged containers. To enable PSA for a namespace in your cluster, set the pod- security.kubernetes.io/enforce label with the policy value you want to enforce. kubectl label --overwrite ns NAMESPACE pod- security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted The above command enforces the restricted policy for the NAMESPACE namespace. You can also enable Pod Security Admission for all your namespaces. For example: kubectl label --overwrite ns --all pod- security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline Internal Only - General Pod Security Policies and Assignments can be found by searching for Policies in the Azure Portal. A detailed step-by-step guide can be found here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/policy-for- kubernetes

check.check-content: List the policies in use for each namespace in the cluster, ensure that each policy disallows the admission of privileged containers. Since manually searching through each pod's configuration might be tedious, especially in environments with many pods, you can use a more automated approach with grep or other command-line tools. Rule.title: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host process ID namespace
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize the admission of pods that request spec.hostPID=true so that only tightly controlled, explicitly approved platform workloads can share the host process ID namespace in AKS. In practice, this means users, groups, and service accounts with deployment rights should not broadly be able to create or update workloads that use host PID sharing, because Microsoft’s AKS identity guidance is to grant identities only the Kubernetes resources they need, and AKS provides Azure Policy and Deployment Safeguards as supported control points for admission governance. Do not generally permit containers to be run with the hostPID flag set to true.
Rationale: A container running in the host's PID namespace can inspect processes running outside the container. If the container also has access to ptrace capabilities this can be used to escalate privileges outside of the container. There should be at least one admission control policy defined which does not permit containers to share the host PID namespace. If you need to run containers which require hostPID, this should be defined in a separate policy and you should carefully check to ensure that only limited service accounts and users are given permission to use that policy.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation=true so that users, groups, and service accounts with deployment rights cannot broadly create pods, init containers, or other workload objects that permit a process to gain more privileges than its parent. In AKS, this remains applicable because Microsoft documents allowPrivilegeEscalation as a pod security context setting that should be designed to stay false, Pod Security Admission is enabled by default, and Azure Policy for AKS includes built-in controls that can set privilege escalation to false at admission time. It's important to note that these rights are still constrained by the overall container sandbox, and this setting does not relate to the use of privileged containers.
Rationale: A container running with the allowPrivilegeEscalation flag set to true may have processes that can gain more privileges than their parent. There should be at least one admission control policy defined which does not permit containers to allow privilege escalation. The option exists (and is defaulted to true) to permit setuid binaries to run. If you have need to run containers which use setuid binaries or require privilege escalation, this should be defined in a separate policy and you should carefully check to ensure that only limited service accounts and users are given permission to use that policy.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure latest Azure CNI Overlay is used
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure the AKS cluster uses Azure CNI Overlay as the supported overlay networking model and remains on current AKS-managed networking components through cluster and node image upgrades. Azure CNI Overlay is the recommended CNI plugin for most overlay scenarios and the general recommendation for pod networking, while AKS delivers related component, feature, and security updates through its managed upgrade model rather than through a separately administered CNI package lifecycle.
Rationale: It is important to maintain a supported and current networking architecture that aligns with Microsoft’s recommended AKS design. Azure CNI Overlay uses a separate pod CIDR, simplifies IP address management, and is identified by Microsoft as the preferred general networking choice for many AKS deployments. Microsoft also states that clusters need updates to newer IPAM modes and data-plane technologies to access the latest features and supportability, which makes staying current on the supported overlay model operationally important even in a managed service.</VulnDiscussion>
