Rule.fixtext: Migrate the cluster to Azure CNI Overlay if it is still using Kubenet or Azure CNI Node Subnet, and complete the change through supported AKS upgrade paths. Microsoft documents a single forward-only migration path to Azure CNI Overlay for existing clusters, and if Azure CNI Powered by Cilium is also required, the IPAM-mode update to Overlay and the data-plane update to Cilium must be performed as separate operations. Configure a supported network policy engine and validate that the cluster network profile to reflect the intended steady state. Microsoft documents Azure CNI Overlay as compatible with supported AKS network policy options, and the remediation should end with confirmation that networkPlugin is Azure, networkPluginMode is Overlay, and the selected policy and data-plane settings match the approved design. • Review the current networkProfile to identify the active network plugin, plugin mode, policy engine, and data plane. • If the cluster is not using Azure CNI Overlay, migrate it using the supported AKS update path for IPAM-mode changes. • If required, perform the data-plane migration to Azure CNI Powered by Cilium as a separate follow-on change. Internal Only - General • Enable or align a supported network policy engine with the approved AKS networking design.

check.check-content: Verify that the AKS cluster is using Azure CNI Overlay as its networking model and that a supported network policy engine is configured as part of the cluster network profile. In current AKS guidance, Azure CNI Overlay is the recommended plugin for most overlay scenarios, and AKS exposes the relevant audit fields through networkProfile, including the network plugin, overlay mode, network policy, and network data plane. Because network-policy capability depends on the configured policy engine and not only on the presence of Azure CNI Overlay, the review should confirm both the overlay configuration and the policy implementation in use. • Confirm the cluster networkProfile shows networkPlugin set to Azure and networkPluginMode set to Overlay. Internal Only - General • Review the networkPolicy setting to verify a supported policy engine is configured rather than none. • Review the networkDataplane value to determine whether the cluster is using the Azure data plane or Cilium, since Microsoft recommends Cilium for new network-policy deployments. • Verify the configured network architecture aligns with current AKS guidance, which recommends Azure CNI Overlay for most overlay scenarios. • Record the returned values as audit evidence and treat the control as not fully satisfied if Overlay is not enabled or if no supported network policy engine is configured. az aks show --resource-group ${RESOURCE_GROUP} --name ${CLUSTER_NAME} --query "{networkPlugin:networkProfile.networkPlugin, networkPluginMode:networkProfile.networkPluginMode, networkPolicy:networkProfile.networkPolicy, networkDataplane:networkProfile.networkDataplane}" -o json Sample Output: { "networkDataplane": "azure", "networkPlugin": "azure", "networkPluginMode": "overlay", "networkPolicy": "azure" } This command returns the key AKS network profile fields needed to determine whether the cluster is using Azure CNI Overlay and whether a supported network policy implementation is enabled.

Rule.title: Ensure that all Namespaces have Network Policies defined
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure each namespace that hosts workloads has explicit NetworkPolicy resources defined so pod ingress and egress behavior is intentionally governed instead of left to the default state. In AKS, Azure CNI Overlay provides direct pod-to-pod communication on an overlay CIDR, and Microsoft documents that pods in an AKS cluster can send and receive traffic without limitations unless network policies are created. Azure CNI Overlay supports Azure network policies, Calico, and Cilium, so this control remains applicable on the current supported overlay model.
Rationale: The rationale is to enforce namespace-level segmentation and least-privilege pod-to- pod traffic control in AKS, where workload communication is unrestricted by default. Microsoft recommends network policies to explicitly define allowed communication paths and reduce unauthorized lateral movement between applications. In Azure CNI Overlay, this is particularly important because the overlay network preserves pod connectivity, but it does not itself enforce workload-level traffic restrictions.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Ensure the AKS cluster is using a supported network policy engine with Azure CNI Overlay, then defining explicit NetworkPolicy objects for every workload-hosting namespace. In AKS, pod traffic is unrestricted by default until policies are applied, Azure CNI Overlay supports Azure network policies, Calico, and Cilium, and Microsoft currently recommends Cilium for new policy deployments because of its scalability, security, and eBPF-based enforcement. 1. Enable or migrate to a supported network policy engine for the cluster if networkPolicy is unset or still using a legacy design. 2. Create a baseline deny-all policy in each workload namespace so traffic is blocked until explicitly allowed. 3. Add targeted ingress and egress allow rules for required application, platform, DNS, logging, and external service flows. 4. Verify that policy podSelector, namespace selectors, ports, and policyTypes cover all intended workloads so pods are not left outside policy scope. 5. Restrict who can create or modify NetworkPolicy resources so namespace segmentation remains controlled and consistent over time. After the policies are deployed, validate that each workload namespace has the required deny and allow rules and confirm application traffic still functions as intended

Rule.title: Prefer exposing secrets as mounted files rather than environment variables
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Prefer exposing secrets to AKS workloads as mounted files rather than as environment variables, particularly when secrets are sourced from Azure Key Vault through the Secrets Store CSI Driver. In current AKS guidance, the Key Vault integration model is volume-based, with secrets made available at a mounted path inside the container, and Microsoft documents that mounted content can be synchronized and rotated through the CSI provider. Environment-variable consumption is still supported when secrets are synced into a Kubernetes Secret, but it is a secondary consumption pattern rather than the native CSI delivery path.
Rationale: It is important to align secret delivery with AKS’s supported rotation and identity model. Microsoft documents that, with autorotation enabled, the CSI provider can update the pod mount and synced Kubernetes Secret, and applications that read secrets from the filesystem can react to file changes without requiring a full pod restart. By contrast, when a secret is consumed as an environment variable, Microsoft states that the pod must be restarted to receive the latest value. In AKS, that makes file-based delivery the stronger pattern for secrets that rotate regularly or are backed by Azure Key Vault.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Move workloads away from secret-backed environment variables and toward file-based secret delivery through mounted volumes, preferably using the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver. In AKS, mounted secrets support sync and autorotation, while secrets exposed through environment variables do not update in running pods until those pods are restarted. 1. Identify workloads that use secretKeyRef or envFrom.secretRef and classify them for migration. Internal Only - General 2. Replace environment-variable injection with mounted secret files, ideally through SecretProviderClass and the Secrets Store CSI Driver. 3. Enable secret autorotation where supported so mounted content and synced Kubernetes Secrets are refreshed automatically. 4. Update the application to read secrets from the mounted path and reload them from file when values change. This last point is an implementation step inferred from Microsoft’s documented mount-update behavior. 5. Keep environment-variable usage only for approved exceptions, and pair those cases with a controlled pod-restart process during secret rotation.

check.check-content: Identify workloads that consume secrets through environment variables and treat those cases as exceptions that require justification. In AKS, mounted secrets are the preferred steady-state pattern because they can be updated through the Secrets Store CSI Driver and autorotation process, whereas secrets exposed through environment variables require a pod restart before updated values are available. This is especially important when secrets are sourced from Azure Key Vault through the managed Secrets Store CSI Driver. Internal Only - General • Identify workloads that use secret-backed environment variables, including secretKeyRef and envFrom.secretRef. • Review whether those workloads use mounted secret files instead of environment-variable injection. • Treat environment-variable usage as an exception and confirm it is documented and justified. • Verify a restart process exists where environment-variable secrets are still required. • Confirm file-based secret delivery is used where rotation is expected. A quick cluster-side verification: kubectl get deploy,statefulset,daemonset,job,cronjob,pod -A -o json | jq -r ' .items[] | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .kind as $kind | .metadata.name as $name | ( if .kind=="CronJob" then .spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec elif .kind=="Pod" then .spec else .spec.template.spec end ) as $spec | [ ($spec.containers[]?.env[]? | select(.valueFrom.secretKeyRef) | "env.secretKeyRef"), ($spec.initContainers[]?.env[]? | select(.valueFrom.secretKeyRef) | "init.env.secretKeyRef"), ($spec.containers[]?.envFrom[]? | select(.secretRef) | "envFrom.secretRef"), ($spec.initContainers[]?.envFrom[]? | select(.secretRef) | "init.envFrom.secretRef") ] | unique | select(length>0) | "\($ns)\t\($kind)/\($name)\t" + join(",") ' NOTE: If the command returns rows, those workloads use secret-backed environment variables and should be reviewed. If it returns no rows, no such references were found in the inspected workloads, but mounted secret volumes or SecretProviderClass usage should still be checked to confirm file-based secret delivery.

Rule.title: Consider external secret storage
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Consider external secret storage for AKS workloads by storing sensitive values in Azure Key Vault and retrieving them at runtime through the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver instead of treating in-cluster Kubernetes Secret objects as the primary secret system. Microsoft documents this as a supported AKS integration in which secrets, keys, and certificates are mounted into pods through a CSI volume, with access mediated by a managed identity or Microsoft Entra Workload ID.
Rationale: It is important to align secret handling with AKS’s supported identity, rotation, and operational model. Microsoft documents that the CSI-based Key Vault integration supports mounted secret delivery, managed identity–based access, autorotation of mounted contents and synced Kubernetes Secrets, and runtime retrieval of the latest secret values from Key Vault. Microsoft’s AKS Well-Architected guidance also states that this pattern helps protect and rotate secrets by using strong encryption, provides an access audit log, and keeps core secrets out of the deployment pipeline.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Move application secrets out of Kubernetes-native storage and deployment artifacts and into Azure Key Vault and then to pods at runtime through the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver. In AKS, pair the CSI driver with Microsoft Entra Workload ID or the add-on managed identity, use mounted secret files as the primary consumption path, and enable autorotation where secret freshness matters. • Inventory secrets currently stored in code, manifests, pipelines, or standalone Kubernetes Secret objects and classify them for migration to Key Vault. • Enable the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver on the cluster if it is not already enabled. • Configure workload access through Workload ID or the AKS-managed identity, with least-privilege Key Vault permissions scoped to only the required secret objects. • Replace secret-backed environment variables with mounted secret files delivered through SecretProviderClass where practical. • Enable secret autorotation for rotatable values and confirm applications can reload updated mounted content without manual secret redistribution.

Microsoft’s current AKS guidance centers on Azure Key Vault, the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver, and mounted secret delivery with autorotation support. • Verify secrets are primarily stored in Azure Key Vault, not embedded in code, manifests, or pipelines. • Confirm the Secrets Store CSI Driver is enabled and SecretProviderClass is used where external secrets are required. Internal Only - General • Review workload access to Key Vault and ensure it uses managed identity or Microsoft Entra Workload ID with least-privilege access. • Flag secret-backed environment variables as exceptions, since mounted secrets support rotation more cleanly. • Verify autorotation is enabled where needed and that applications can reload updated mounted secrets.

Rule.title: Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Create administrative boundaries between resources by organizing AKS workloads into separate namespaces and scoping access to those namespaces with Kubernetes RBAC or Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. Namespaces form the logical isolation boundary for workloads and resources, and Kubernetes RBAC can scope permissions to a single namespace or across the entire cluster. In AKS, this is the standard way to separate teams, applications, and environments inside a shared cluster while applying per-namespace controls such as access, quotas, and network policy.
Rationale: It is important to reduce administrative sprawl and enforce least-privilege operations within a shared AKS cluster. Microsoft recommends logical isolation first because it lets multiple workloads or teams share one cluster while still applying scoped permissions and other namespace-level controls, which improves density and reduces excess capacity compared with creating separate clusters for every team or application. Namespace scoping also fits Microsoft’s identity guidance, which emphasizes granting users, groups, and service accounts only the resources they need. Limiting the scope of user permissions reduces the impact of mistakes or malicious activity by keeping administrative access aligned to a defined namespace boundary. In AKS, namespaces provide logical separation for workloads and resources, and access to those namespaces can be controlled through Kubernetes RBAC or Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. While resources are created in the default namespace unless another namespace is specified, Microsoft’s current guidance is to organize workloads into separate namespaces and apply scoped access, quotas, and network policies to support controlled multi-team or multi-application operations within a shared cluster.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Microsoft recommends namespaces as the logical isolation boundary for workloads and resources in shared clusters, combined with namespace-level governance such as quotas and network policies; where stronger tenant isolation is required, Microsoft recommends separate clusters rather than relying on namespaces alone. 1. Create separate namespaces for each team, application, or environment that requires its own administrative scope. 2. Move workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespace structure. 3. Rebind access using namespace-scoped Role and RoleBinding objects, or namespace-scoped Azure RBAC assignments where applicable. 4. Apply namespace-level controls such as resource quotas and network policies to reinforce the administrative boundary. 5. Remove unused namespaces and reduce cluster-wide permissions that bypass intended namespace separation. Internal Only - General

check.check-content: Verify that namespaces are not only present, but are being used as intentional administrative boundaries for teams, applications, or environments within the AKS cluster. Namespaces are the logical isolation boundary for workloads and resources in a shared cluster, and they should be paired with scoped access controls and other namespace-level governance such as quotas and network policies. Namespaces alone are not sufficient for hostile multitenancy, so the audit should focus on whether they are being used consistently to separate administration and operations as intended. • List all namespaces in the cluster and confirm each one has a defined administrative or workload purpose. • Verify that user and service-account access is scoped to the appropriate namespaces rather than granted broadly at cluster scope. • Review whether namespace-level controls such as quotas and network policies are applied where required. Quick inventory checks: kubectl get namespaces kubectl get rolebindings,roles -A kubectl get clusterrolebindings,clusterroles kubectl get resourcequota,networkpolicy -A A namespace should be considered adequately administered only when it has a clear purpose, appropriately scoped RBAC, and the namespace-level controls needed for that workload or team.

Rule.title: Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Apply securityContext settings to pods and containers so workload runtime behavior is explicitly constrained instead of relying on image defaults or permissive cluster admission. In AKS, Microsoft’s current pod-security guidance calls out settings such as runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities, and seccompProfile, and AKS supports enforcing or validating these expectations through Pod Security Admission and Deployment Safeguards.
Rationale: Applying securityContext reduces container runtime privilege and strengthens isolation between the application and the host. It helps enforce least-privilege execution by avoiding root access, limiting unnecessary privilege escalation, and supporting Linux security controls such as user namespaces, AppArmor, and seccomp. In AKS, these restrictions are defined in the workload manifest and carried consistently into deployment.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Remediate by defining and enforcing a hardened pod/container security baseline for all application namespaces in AKS, then requiring workloads to declare the necessary securityContext fields in their manifests. In AKS, Pod Security Admission (PSA) is enabled by default and is applied with namespace labels, while Microsoft’s pod-security guidance recommends explicit settings such as non-root execution, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, limited capabilities, and seccompProfile. For broader cluster-wide governance, AKS also supports Deployment Safeguards to warn on or deny noncompliant workload definitions at create or update time. • Apply PSA restricted or baseline labels to general application namespaces, using warn and audit first where rollout needs to be staged. • Update workload manifests to define pod- and container-level securityContext values such as runAsNonRoot, explicit user/group IDs where required, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, dropped capabilities, and seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. • Restrict exception workloads to tightly controlled namespaces and service accounts, and limit who can deploy there through namespace-scoped RBAC. This follows AKS’s logical-isolation and least-privilege model. • Use Deployment Safeguards where centralized warn-or-deny enforcement is needed for pod security settings. • Revalidate workloads after rollout to confirm required applications still function without broad privilege, root execution, or unnecessary host access. This implementation step follows from Microsoft’s guidance to limit containers to only the actions and permissions they need.

check.check-content: Audit this control by reviewing workload manifests to confirm pod- and container-level securityContext settings are explicitly defined and aligned to the AKS security baseline. Focus on runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities, and seccompProfile. • Flag workloads that run as root, allow privilege escalation, or omit required security context controls as findings unless formally approved. Microsoft specifically recommends setting allowPrivilegeEscalation to false and running as a defined non-root user or group. Rule.title: The default namespace should not be used
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Avoid placing application workloads in the default namespace, and instead deploy them into dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended team, application, or environment boundary. In AKS, namespaces are the built-in way to logically divide cluster resources and scope access, while the default namespace exists mainly so a cluster can be used immediately without first creating a new namespace. Microsoft’s current AKS namespace guidance also ties namespace design to per-namespace controls such as RBAC, quotas, and network policies.
Rationale: It is important to preserve least-privilege administration and make namespace-scoped governance actually usable. Namespaces form the logical isolation boundary in shared clusters, and AKS RBAC can scope permissions to a single namespace instead of the whole cluster. When workloads stay in default, it becomes harder to apply clean administrative separation, delegated access, resource quotas, and namespace-level network segmentation in the way AKS is designed to support.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Create purpose-specific namespaces for teams, applications, and environments, then require all new resources to be deployed into those namespaces instead of default. In AKS, namespaces are the logical boundary for workload administration, so remediation should include migrating existing resources into managed namespaces, applying namespace-scoped RBAC and other controls, and reserving cluster-wide access for true platform administrators only.

check.check-content: Verify that the default namespace is not being used as a landing zone for user- managed applications, supporting resources, or namespace-scoped identities. In AKS, namespaces are the logical administrative boundary for workloads, and Microsoft flags use of the default namespace as a security recommendation because it can expose common namespace-scoped resource types to broader-than-intended access. A namespace should pass this control only when application resources have been moved into dedicated namespaces and default is not being used for normal workload administration. • List resources in the default namespace and identify any user-managed workloads or supporting objects. • Review whether application resources, service accounts, ConfigMaps, and Secrets are being created in default instead of dedicated namespaces. Internal Only - General • Treat any non-exempt application use of default as a finding, even if the namespace also contains expected cluster-created objects. • Confirm user and service-account access is scoped to purpose-built namespaces rather than relying on default for routine operations. kubectl get pod,svc,configmap,secret,serviceaccount,deploy,statefulset,daemonset,job,cron job,ingress -n default

Rule.title: Ensure container image vulnerability scanning with Defender for Containers or a third-party provider
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Ensure vulnerability scanning is enabled for container images that are stored in registries and intended for deployment to AKS, using Microsoft Defender for Containers in Defender for Cloud or an equivalent third-party scanner. This control applies both to registry images and, where enabled and supported, to running containers in AKS. For Defender-based coverage, registry image assessment requires Registry access to be enabled, and Microsoft documents support for scanning images in ACR and other supported registries; scans occur for newly pushed or imported images and are continuously re-run for recent or currently running images so findings remain current as new CVEs are published.
Rationale: It is important to reduce software supply chain risk before vulnerable images are deployed or continue running in AKS. Container images should be scanned for vulnerabilities and only validated images should be deployed. Defender for Containers adds technical depth by performing agentless vulnerability assessment across supported container images, including OS packages and supported language packages, and then surfacing CVE findings and remediation guidance through Defender for Cloud recommendations. This makes image scanning a preventive control for AKS rather than only a post-deployment detection mechanism.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Enable Microsoft Defender for Containers for the subscription, enable the registry vulnerability assessment capability used for container image scanning, and then verify that Defender for Cloud is producing vulnerability findings for the registries and AKS workloads in scope. If the control is intended to cover only registry image scanning, the subscription plan and registry access settings are the key fixes; if it also includes AKS runtime protection, deploy the Defender sensor or AKS built-in integration and confirm the cluster Defender profile is enabled. 1. In the Defender for Cloud Environment settings turn Containers from Free to Standard. 2. Enable the registry image assessment capability by turning on the registry- related extension, including ContainerRegistriesVulnerabilityAssessments and required Registry access for supported registries.a 3. For AKS cluster-side coverage, deploy the Defender sensor by using the AKS built-in option or Helm, based on your deployment model. 4. Recheck the cluster and confirm securityProfile.defender.securityMonitoring.enabled is true where AKS runtime monitoring is required. 5. Review Defender for Cloud recommendations, then rebuild, patch, or replace vulnerable images and revalidate until findings reflect the intended state. Verification commands: az security pricing show --name Containers -o json az aks show --resource-group ${RESOURCE_GROUP} --name ${CLUSTER_NAME} --query "securityProfile.defender" -o json

For AKS, also verify the cluster Defender profile when cluster-side monitoring is in scope, and confirm Defender for Cloud is generating vulnerability findings for relevant images. • Confirm Microsoft.Security/pricings/Containers uses pricingTier: Standard. • Confirm the ContainerRegistriesVulnerabilityAssessments extension is enabled. To verify the cluster side directly, use: az aks show --resource-group ${RESOURCE_GROUP} --name ${CLUSTER_NAME} --query "securityProfile.defender" -o json The expected result should include securityMonitoring.enabled set to true. To verify the subscription plan more broadly use: az security pricing show --name Containers -o json That should show the plan on Standard when Defender for Containers is enabled.

Rule.title: Minimize and scope access to Azure Container Registry
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Limit ACR access for AKS and related users to only the permissions required for their function. AKS-to-ACR integration grants the cluster’s kubelet managed identity the AcrPull role so nodes can pull images without broader registry rights for ABAC-enabled registries using the Container Registry Repository Reader role instead. Human users, CI/CD identities, and applications should be assigned only the minimum pull, push, or repository-scoped rights they need through Microsoft Entra RBAC or ABAC, and the ACR admin account should remain disabled unless there is a specific operational need for it.
Rationale: Restricting ACR access reduces the chance that a user or workload can push unapproved images, overwrite trusted tags, read images from repositories outside its scope, or rely on long-lived shared credentials. Managed identities over service principals in AKS because Azure manages the credentials and rotation, which removes secret-handling overhead and lowers credential exposure. ACR also supports repository-level scoping with Microsoft Entra ABAC, which helps enforce least privilege more precisely than broad registry-wide assignments.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Disable the ACR local admin account and use identity-based, least-privilege access for registry authentication and authorization. For AKS, use the kubelet managed identity for required image pull access, and assign only the minimum registry role required by the registry authorization model: AcrPull for non-ABAC registries or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC-enabled registries. Human users, pipelines, and other workloads should use Microsoft Entra service principals, managed identities, or repository-scoped permissions only where additional access is operationally required, rather than shared local registry credentials. • Identify any scripts, pipelines, or workloads that still depend on the ACR admin username and password. • Assign the AKS kubelet identity only the required pull role. • Remove unnecessary push, delete, catalog, or admin permissions from other principals. • Disable the ACR local admin account. • Re-test image pull and push operations after the change. • Recheck the registry and confirm adminUserEnabled returns false. az acr show --name ${ACR_NAME} --resource-group ${RESOURCE_GROUP} --query "adminUserEnabled" -o tsv az acr update --name ${ACR_NAME} --resource-group ${RESOURCE_GROUP} --admin- enabled false Expected result after remediation: adminUserEnabled should return false.

check.check-content: Review ACR access for AKS to confirm the registry uses least-privilege, identity-based access. Verify the ACR admin account is disabled, determine whether the registry is using RBAC only or RBAC + ABAC, confirm the AKS kubelet identity has only image pull rights, and review other principals for unnecessary push, delete, or broader registry permissions. • Confirm that adminUserEnabled is false, since the local admin account provides broad registry access and is not the preferred authentication method for AKS-integrated ACR use. Internal Only - General az acr show --name ${ACR_NAME} --resource-group ${RESOURCE_GROUP} --query "adminUserEnabled" -o tsv • Review roleAssignmentMode to determine whether the registry uses rbac or rbac-abac, because ABAC-enabled registries use repository-scoped authorization and different expected pull-role assignments. • Verify that the AKS kubelet managed identity has only the minimum pull role required: AcrPull for non-ABAC registries, or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC-enabled registries. • Review ACR role assignments for users, groups, service principals, and managed identities, and identify any principals with unnecessary push, delete, catalog, or registry administration permissions. • For ABAC-enabled registries, review repository conditions and scope restrictions to confirm access is limited to the required repositories or repository paths.

Rule.title: Minimize AKS cluster access to pull-only access for Azure Container Registry
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Configure AKS with read-only access to ACR so the cluster can pull the images it needs to run workloads without being able to modify registry content. This is implemented by granting the kubelet managed identity only the required pull permission—typically AcrPull for non-ABAC registries, or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC- enabled registries—so cluster access is limited to image retrieval rather than push, delete, or registry administration actions.
Rationale: Restricting AKS to read-only registry access enforces least privilege and reduces the blast radius of a compromised node identity or misused cluster credential. Using managed identities instead of service principals allows Azure to manage credential issuance and rotation, which avoids stored secrets and reduces operational exposure. Limiting the kubelet identity to pull-only access also prevents the cluster from modifying repository content, overwriting tags, or using broader registry permissions than required for normal image retrieval.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Restrict AKS access to ACR so the cluster can only pull images needed for workload startup and cannot push, delete, or administer registry content. For AKS, this means using the kubelet managed identity for registry authentication and assigning only the minimum pull role required by the registry authorization mode: AcrPull for non-ABAC registries or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC-enabled registries. 1. Configure AKS to use the kubelet managed identity for ACR access rather than shared registry credentials. 2. Assign only the required pull role to the kubelet identity: AcrPull for standard RBAC registries, or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC- enabled registries. 3. Remove any additional ACR permissions granted to the kubelet identity, especially write, delete, or broader registry management roles. 4. For ABAC-enabled registries, scope repository-reader access only to the required repositories or repository paths where possible.

check.check-content: Review AKS access to ACR to confirm the cluster is limited to image pull access and does not have broader registry permissions. Identify the registry authorization mode, confirm the kubelet managed identity is used for ACR access, and verify that the cluster has only the minimum read role required for image pulls. • Determine whether the registry uses RBAC Registry Permissions or RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions, because this affects the expected pull role and scope model. • Verify that AKS authenticates to ACR with the kubelet managed identity rather than stored registry credentials or broad shared access. • Confirm that the kubelet identity has only the required read role: AcrPull for non-ABAC registries, or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC- enabled registries. Internal Only - General • Review ACR role assignments for the kubelet identity and confirm no additional push, delete, or registry administration permissions are assigned at the registry or repository scope.

Rule.title: Restrict AKS workloads to approved container registries only
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Configure AKS so workloads pull images only from registries that have been explicitly approved by the organization, such as selected ACR instances or other trusted registries. In AKS, this is typically enforced with Azure Policy by auditing or denying deployments that reference images outside the approved registry list, while AKS-to- ACR integration provides the managed identity and pull-role pattern needed for authorized image retrieval from those registries.
Rationale: Limiting AKS to approved registries reduces the chance that pods will run images from unknown, unvetted, or malicious sources. In AKS image-management only validates images that should be deployed, and the AKS built-in policy for allowed images is specifically intended to reduce exposure to unknown vulnerabilities, security issues, and malicious images from untrusted registries.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Restrict AKS workloads to approved container registries by enforcing an Azure Policy control for allowed images or trusted registries, defining the approved registry list, and ensuring workloads reference only those registries. In AKS, using the Azure Policy add- on with built-in AKS policies, and AKS image-management guidance recommends deploying only validated images. 1. Enable the Azure Policy add-on on the AKS cluster if it is not already installed. 2. Assign an AKS policy or initiative that audits or denies unapproved image sources, and set the parameters to the organization’s approved registry list. 3. Migrate or mirror workload images from external or nonapproved registries into an approved registry, such as ACR, before deployment. AKS-to-ACR integration supports authenticated image pulls through the kubelet managed identity. 4. Update manifests, Helm charts, and CI/CD pipelines so image references point only to approved registries, then validate policy compliance and redeploy affected workloads.

check.check-content: Review AKS image source controls to confirm workloads are limited to approved container registries. The audit should verify that an Azure Policy definition or initiative is assigned to the cluster to audit or deny unapproved image sources, that the approved registry list is explicitly defined, and that AKS has valid pull access only to those approved registries. In addition, deploy only validated images which supports restricting image sources to trusted registries. • Verify that the Azure Policy add-on is installed on the AKS cluster and that a built-in policy for allowed container images or trusted registries is assigned. • Review the policy parameters to confirm the approved registry list is explicitly defined and reflects the registries authorized for AKS workload deployment. • Inspect sample workload manifests or deployed pods to confirm image references resolve only to approved registries, such as designated ACR instances or other trusted sources. Internal Only - General • Verify that AKS has pull permissions only to the approved registries needed for workload deployment, using the expected AKS-to-registry authentication model for those registries.

Group.title: 5.2 Access and identity options for Azure Kubernetes Service

Rule.title: Prefer using dedicated AKS Service Accounts
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>It is important to use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts in AKS so identity, permissions, and token use are isolated to the specific workload that requires them, rather than shared across unrelated pods. In AKS, service accounts remain a core Kubernetes identity construct and also serve as the anchor for Microsoft Entra Workload ID, which allows access to Kubernetes and Azure resources to be scoped per workload.
Rationale: Using dedicated service accounts supports least privilege by allowing each AKS workload to receive only the Kubernetes RBAC permissions and Azure access it actually requires, instead of sharing identity and permissions through a common account. It also helps limit token exposure and lateral movement, because access to Secrets can expose service account credentials, and unnecessary token mounting increases the number of workloads that carry usable credentials.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT
reference.dc:subject: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT

Rule.fixtext: Use a dedicated Kubernetes service account for each AKS workload that requires identity, and replace use of the namespace default service account wherever it is not explicitly required. Scope each service account to only the Kubernetes permissions and Azure resource access needed by that workload, and prevent service account tokens from being mounted into pods unless token-based access is required. 1. Create a separate Kubernetes service account for each workload or application boundary that requires distinct access. 2. Bind each service account only to the minimum required Kubernetes Role or ClusterRole, and avoid granting custom permissions to the namespace default service account. 3. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods that do not need a service account token. 4. If a workload needs access to Azure resources, enable the AKS OIDC issuer and Microsoft Entra Workload ID, create the federated identity credential, and annotate the dedicated service account for that workload. 5. Update Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs, and other controllers so they reference the intended dedicated service account.

check.check-content: For each namespace, verify that workloads do not use the default service account unless required, and confirm that the default service account has no custom role bindings beyond baseline defaults. Review workload-specific service accounts to ensure permissions are scoped with least privilege, and confirm automountServiceAccountToken is disabled where token access is not needed. • Review each namespace for pods and workload controllers that use the default service account, and flag any use that is not explicitly required, because dedicated service accounts are the workload identity boundary in AKS. • Review RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments for the default service account and confirm it has no custom permissions beyond baseline defaults; then verify workload-specific service accounts are bound only to the minimum required RBAC roles. • Check service accounts and pod specs for unnecessary token exposure, and confirm automountServiceAccountToken is set to false where a workload does not need a service account token. Internal Only - General • For workloads that access Azure resources, verify they use a dedicated Kubernetes service account with the expected workload identity configuration, including service account annotation and federated identity mapping, rather than a shared or default account.

Rule.title: Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets at rest with AKS KMS protection
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Kubernetes Secret data stored by AKS in etcd must be protected with encryption at rest, and, when mapped to Key Management Service, that protection should be implemented through the AKS KMS provider integrated with Azure Key Vault. In AKS, Azure platform encryption remains the baseline storage-layer protection, while KMS adds envelope encryption of Kubernetes secrets before they are committed to etcd. In addition, AKS KMS supports either platform-managed keys for simpler operation or customer- managed keys in Azure Key Vault when you need direct control over the encryption key lifecycle.
Rationale: AKS stores Kubernetes Secret objects in etcd, so encrypting them adds protection beyond the baseline Azure storage-layer encryption. When AKS KMS is used, secrets are encrypted before being written to etcd, with Azure Key Vault protecting the encryption key material through envelope encryption.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT
reference.dc:subject: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT

Rule.fixtext: For AKS clusters that do not use KMS for Kubernetes Secret encryption, enable AKS KMS so Secret data is encrypted before it is written to etcd. AKS distinguishes this from the baseline Azure platform encryption that is always on at the storage layer, and documents AKS KMS as the added Azure Key Vault–backed encryption layer for Kubernetes secrets. For newer supported clusters, use the current KMS data-encryption model; where customer-managed keys are required, configure the Azure Key Vault key, assign the required managed identity and permissions, enable KMS on the cluster, and then verify the cluster security profile reflects the expected KMS settings. 1. Identify AKS clusters where KMS is not enabled for Kubernetes Secret encryption, using cluster configuration review or Azure Policy. 2. Decide whether to use platform-managed keys or customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault based on the organization’s key ownership and compliance requirements. 3. For customer-managed key deployments, create or select the Azure Key Vault key, assign a user-managed identity, and grant the identity the required key permissions before enabling KMS. 4. If a private Key Vault is used, also configure the required private-access settings and confirm the cluster identity can reach and use the vault, because AKS does not automatically validate those permissions in that scenario. 5. After remediation, validate that the AKS securityProfile shows KMS enabled and the expected Key Vault key configuration, and confirm the referenced vault and key remain available to avoid loss of access to encrypted secrets.

check.check-content: Review each AKS cluster in scope to determine whether Key Management Service (KMS) encryption for Kubernetes Secrets is enabled and correctly configured. Note the Azure platform encryption is always enabled for data at rest, but AKS KMS adds a separate encryption layer that encrypts Kubernetes Secret data before it is written to etcd by using Azure Key Vault–backed keys. As part of the audit, verify that the cluster security profile shows AKS KMS enabled, confirm the configured key identifier and Key Vault settings are present and valid, and ensure the referenced Key Vault and key have not been deleted or expired. Where private Key Vault mode is used, also verify the cluster identity still has the required access because Microsoft notes AKS cannot automatically validate those permissions for private vault scenarios. Use the following command to inspect the KMS configuration for a specific cluster: Internal Only - General az aks show \ --name $CLUSTER_NAME \ --resource-group $RESOURCE_GROUP \ --query "{KmsEnabled:securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms.enabled,KeyId:securityProfile.a zureKeyVaultKms.keyId,KeyVaultNetworkAccess:securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms. keyVaultNetworkAccess,KeyVaultResourceId:securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms.key VaultResourceId}" \ -o json The cluster should show KmsEnabled as true, and the output should include the expected Azure Key Vault key reference in KeyId. If the cluster uses a private Key Vault, the audit should also confirm the expected private vault resource ID and network access mode are populated.

Rule.title: Restrict Access to the Control Plane Endpoint
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The AKS control plane endpoint should be exposed only through approved network paths rather than being broadly reachable. In AKS, the control plane is the Kubernetes API server. For public clusters, API server authorized IP ranges can be used to limit access to specific public IP addresses or CIDR blocks and deny all other sources. For more restrictive deployments, AKS also supports private clusters, where the API server is exposed through a private endpoint with private DNS resolution, and API Server VNet Integration, which keeps API server connectivity on private network paths within the virtual network.
Rationale: In AKS, the Kubernetes API server is assigned a public IP address by default, so restricting access to approved source IP addresses reduces exposure of the control plane to unsolicited network traffic. API server authorized IP ranges allow only specified public IP addresses or CIDR blocks to reach the public API server endpoint, while requests from other source IPs are blocked. For environments that do not permit internet-reachable management endpoints, Microsoft recommends using a private cluster so API server access stays on private network paths instead of relying on public endpoint filtering alone.</VulnDiscussion>

reference.dc:title: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT
reference.dc:subject: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Benchmark - DRAFT

Rule.fixtext: If the cluster is intended to expose the Kubernetes API server only over private network paths, use a private AKS cluster; if the cluster is already private but a public DNS name is still published, disable the public FQDN. If the cluster must keep a public API server endpoint, configure authorized IP ranges so only approved administrator and egress CIDR ranges can reach it. Microsoft notes that authorized IP ranges apply only to the public API server endpoint, recommends including both the cluster egress IP and the networks used to administer the cluster, and states that rule updates can take up to two minutes to propagate. 1. If enablePrivateCluster is false and the cluster should be managed only over private connectivity, move to private cluster mode using the Microsoft- supported private-cluster workflow for that cluster type; Microsoft documents enablement on supported existing clusters with API Server VNet integration and private-cluster deployment for new clusters. 2. If enablePrivateCluster is true but enablePublicFqdn is also true and your standard does not allow a public DNS name, disable the public FQDN for the private cluster. 3. If the cluster keeps a public API server endpoint and authorizedIpRanges is empty or null, add approved CIDR ranges so the API server is not broadly reachable from the internet. 4. If authorizedIpRanges is present but incomplete, update it to include only the required administrator, VPN, firewall, NAT gateway, and other approved egress ranges including the cluster egress IP and the networks from which the cluster is administered. 5. After remediation, rerun the same az aks show audit query and test access from both approved and nonapproved network paths, allowing for the documented propagation delay before confirming results.

check.check-content: Review each AKS cluster to determine how the Kubernetes API server is exposed and whether network-based restrictions are configured appropriately. Specifically, verify whether the cluster is deployed as a private cluster, whether a public FQDN remains enabled for that private cluster, and whether authorized IP ranges are configured on any public API server endpoint. In AKS, authorized IP ranges apply to the public API server endpoint, while private-cluster access is controlled through private networking and DNS design rather than public IP allowlisting. export CLUSTER_NAME=<your cluster name> export RESOURCE_GROUP=<your resource group name> az aks show \ --name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \ --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \ --query "{enablePrivateCluster:apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster, enablePublicFqdn:apiServerAccessProfile.enablePublicFqdn, authorizedIpRanges:apiServerAccessProfile.authorizedIpRanges}" \ --output json Interpretation: • enablePrivateCluster: true means the cluster is configured as a private AKS cluster and the API server is intended to be reached through private network connectivity. • enablePublicFqdn: true means a public DNS name exists for the API server in that cluster configuration; for private clusters, Microsoft documents that both private and public FQDNs are created by default unless the public FQDN is disabled. This setting should not be described as “endpointPublicAccess.” • authorizedIpRanges lists the allowed source CIDR ranges for access to the public API server endpoint. If the list is empty or null on a public cluster, there is no IP-based restriction on that public endpoint. On a private cluster, these ranges do not secure the private API endpoint itself. The result for a private cluster should show enablePrivateCluster as true. enablePublicFqdn should be evaluated against your security standard, and authorizedIpRanges should only be treated as relevant where a public API server endpoint is in play. For a public cluster, the key networking control is whether authorizedIpRanges is populated with only approved administrator or egress CIDR blocks. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Use private AKS clusters and disable public control plane DNS
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Provisioning AKS in private cluster mode limits control plane exposure by placing the Kubernetes API server on private addressing and requiring connectivity through Azure Private Link and a private endpoint rather than broad public network access. In this design, AKS creates the private endpoint and supporting private DNS integration needed for internal name resolution, and the public FQDN can also be disabled when the security requirement is to prevent the control plane from publishing any public DNS name. This reduces the external attack surface of the cluster management plane and aligns API server access to approved private network paths only.
Rationale: Because the AKS API server is public by default, provisioning the cluster in private cluster mode materially reduces control plane exposure by shifting API server access from internet-routable paths to Azure Private Link, private endpoint connectivity, and private DNS resolution. This constrains administrative access to approved internal network paths and reduces dependence on public endpoint protections alone. Disabling the public FQDN provides additional hardening because private AKS clusters otherwise publish both private and public DNS names by default.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Use the apiServerAccessProfile results to determine whether the cluster must be moved to private cluster mode and whether the public FQDN must be disabled. Remediation should bring the cluster to enablePrivateCluster: true and, where required by policy, enablePublicFqdn: false; the detailed action depends on whether the cluster is new or existing and whether API Server VNet Integration is already in place. 1. If enablePrivateCluster is false on a new deployment, create the cluster as private by using az aks create --enable-private-cluster add --disable- public-fqdn when the requirement is to prevent publication of a public DNS name for the API server. Internal Only - General 2. If enablePrivateCluster is false on an existing cluster, first determine whether the cluster already uses API Server VNet Integration. Microsoft states that clusters with API Server VNet Integration can have private cluster mode enabled without redeployment; the documented update path is az aks update --enable-private-cluster --enable-apiserver-vnet-integration -- apiserver-subnet-id <subnet-id>. 3. If API Server VNet Integration must be enabled on an existing cluster first, plan for the documented operational effects: the feature is one-way, requires an immediate cluster restart after enablement, performs a rolling node-image upgrade, and can change the API server IP address even though the hostname stays the same. 4. If enablePrivateCluster is true but enablePublicFqdn is true, disable the public FQDN by running az aks update --disable-public-fqdn against the private cluster. 5. After remediation, rerun the audit command and confirm enablePrivateCluster is true and enablePublicFqdn is false then validate that private DNS resolution and approved private network paths can still reach the API server.

check.check-content: Review the AKS cluster apiServerAccessProfile to confirm the control plane is deployed as a private AKS cluster and that the public FQDN is disabled when the security standard requires no public DNS name for the Kubernetes API server. In AKS, a private cluster uses internal IP addressing for the API server and private connectivity through Azure Private Link and a private endpoint. In addition, private AKS clusters create both private and public FQDNs by default unless the public FQDN is explicitly disabled. Internal Only - General export CLUSTER_NAME=<your cluster name> export RESOURCE_GROUP=<your resource group name> az aks show \ --name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \ --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \ --query "{enablePrivateCluster:apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster, enablePublicFqdn:apiServerAccessProfile.enablePublicFqdn, authorizedIpRanges:apiServerAccessProfile.authorizedIpRanges}" \ --output json Output should be similar to: { "enablePrivateCluster": true, "enablePublicFqdn": false, "authorizedIpRanges": null } • enablePrivateCluster should be true to show the cluster is deployed in private cluster mode. Microsoft states that, in a private cluster, the control plane or API server uses internal IP addresses and communicates with the cluster through Azure Private Link and a private endpoint. • enablePublicFqdn should be false when the requirement is to prevent the API server from publishing a public DNS name. Microsoft documents that private AKS clusters create both private and public FQDNs by default unless the public FQDN is disabled. • authorizedIpRanges is not the primary compliance check for this control. Microsoft states that authorized IP ranges apply only to the public API server endpoint and can’t be applied to the private API server endpoint. • If enablePrivateCluster is false, the cluster does not meet this control because the API server isn’t restricted to private-cluster connectivity. • If enablePrivateCluster is true but enablePublicFqdn is also true, the cluster is private but still publishes a public DNS name, so it would not meet a stricter requirement that public control plane naming be disabled.

Rule.title: Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In AKS, node pools should use private IP addressing only and should not assign instance-level public IPs to individual nodes unless a specific workload requires that design. Keeping nodes private reduces direct internet reachability of the worker node plane and helps ensure node access occurs through approved internal network paths, load-balanced services, or controlled management methods rather than through per- node public exposure.
Rationale: In AKS, assigning an instance-level public IP to each node pool VM makes the worker node plane directly internet-routable, which increases exposure beyond the standard AKS networking model. AKS nodes do not require their own public IP addresses for normal cluster communication, so enabling enableNodePublicIP is a deliberate exception rather than a default requirement. Keeping nodes on private IPs preserves the intended separation between node infrastructure, workload ingress, and cluster egress, where external access is normally handled through Kubernetes Services, load balancers, ingress, or other controlled network paths instead of direct per-node addressing.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Where AKS node pools are configured with node public IPs, the preferred remediation is to return them to the standard AKS networking model unless there is a clear workload requirement for direct per-node public reachability. In AKS, node public IPs are an optional feature rather than the normal operating model, so remediation should focus on removing unnecessary node-level internet exposure and shifting any needed inbound or outbound connectivity to supported service and egress patterns. 1. Identify each node pool where enableNodePublicI P is enabled and confirm whether the setting is actually required for the workload, since AKS documents node public IPs as a special-case feature. 2. For node pools that do not require direct node-level public reachability, update the node pool configuration to disable node public IPs by removing the -- enable-node-public-ip setting from the intended state and applying the supported AKS node-pool update path. 3. If the workload needs inbound exposure, replace direct node addressing with supported Kubernetes or Azure exposure methods such as Services, ingress, or load balancer front ends instead of keeping public IPs on individual nodes. Internal Only - General 4. If the workload needs stable outbound source addresses, use an AKS-supported egress design such as configured outbound IPs on the Standard Load Balancer rather than assigning public IPs to each node. 5. After remediation, rerun the node-pool audit and confirm each in-scope pool reports enableNodePublicIP: false.

check.check-content: Review each AKS node pool to determine whether node public IPs are enabled. In AKS, this control is a node-pool setting, not a control-plane setting, and node public IP as an optional feature for special scenarios rather than a normal requirement the default value for enableNodePublicIP is false. Use this command to audit all node pools in the cluster: Internal Only - General export CLUSTER_NAME=<your cluster name> export RESOURCE_GROUP=<your resource group name> az aks show \ --name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \ --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \ --query "agentPoolProfiles[].{nodePool:name,mode:mode,enableNodePublicIP:enableNodePu blicIP}" \ --output json The result should show enableNodePublicIP: false for every node pool unless there is a documented exception for a specific workload. In AKS, nodes do not require their own public IP addresses for normal communication, and the Azure AKS resource model documents enableNodePublicIP with a default of false. • Verify every system and user node pool returned by the command, because a single node pool with enableNodePublicIP: true means that pool’s nodes are configured with instance-level public IPs. • Treat enableNodePublicIP: false as the expected value for compliant node pools. • Treat any node pool with enableNodePublicIP: true as an exception requiring documented justification, since Microsoft describes node public IPs as an optional feature for specific scenarios. • Do not use apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster to audit this control, because that checks private control plane access, not whether worker nodes have public IPs. This control is audited from the node pool configuration.

Rule.title: Ensure Network Policy is Enabled and set as appropriate
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In AKS, the cluster should have a supported network policy engine enabled and the resulting policy model should be configured to enforce the intended pod-level traffic restrictions. Network policies in AKS are used to allow or deny traffic between pods based on selectors such as namespace, labels, and ports. AKS documentation lists Cilium, Azure Network Policy Manager (NPM), and Calico as AKS network policy options, while also documenting that Azure CNI Powered by Cilium can enforce network policies without installing a separate policy engine and is the recommended path for new Linux deployments.
Rationale: In AKS, pod traffic is permitted by default unless network policy enforcement is enabled, so workloads can communicate laterally across namespaces and application tiers without pod-level restriction. Enabling network policy adds a Kubernetes-native enforcement layer that filters ingress and egress traffic between pods by using label, namespace, and port-based rules, which is the technical mechanism AKS uses for east- west micro segmentation. This allows the cluster to restrict traffic paths to only those required by the application design, instead of relying on unrestricted pod-to-pod communication.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Align each AKS cluster to an approved network policy baseline based on the networkProfile audit results. If networkPolicy is none or null, enable a supported policy capability so pod-to-pod traffic is no longer unmanaged by default. For new Linux- based AKS deployments, the preferred target state is Azure CNI Powered by Cilium with Cilium network policy, because it provides Kubernetes-native policy enforcement on an eBPF dataplane and is the recommended direction for new deployments. For existing clusters, treat remediation as a planned networking migration and standardization effort. Move clusters from nonpreferred engines to the approved target state, validate policy behavior after the change, and stage the migration when the cluster must first move to a different Azure CNI IPAM mode before adopting the target dataplane. The remediation end state should be an AKS configuration where the selected policy engine and dataplane are both supported, intentional, and matched to the cluster’s operating system and networking design.

check.check-content: Review the AKS cluster networkProfile to verify that a supported network policy capability is enabled and that the configured policy model matches the cluster’s networking design. In current AKS, networkProfile.networkPolicy can be azure, calico, cilium, or none, and networkProfile.networkDataplane can be azure or cilium. Because modern AKS Cilium-based deployments use the Cilium dataplane, the audit should evaluate both fields together instead of checking networkPolicy alone. Run this command: Internal Only - General export CLUSTER_NAME=<your cluster name> export RESOURCE_GROUP=<your resource group name> az aks show \ --name "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \ --resource-group "${RESOURCE_GROUP}" \ --query "{networkPolicy:networkProfile.networkPolicy,networkDataplane:networkProfile. networkDataplane,networkPlugin:networkProfile.networkPlugin,networkPluginMode :networkProfile.networkPluginMode}" \ --output json The results should show networkPolicy set to an approved value rather than null or none If your standard prefers or requires Cilium, the expected result should also show networkDataplane: "cilium". Microsoft’s current AKS documentation also states that pods can communicate without limitation by default, so a result showing no active network policy capability should be treated as noncompliant unless there is a documented exception. Output results would show: • networkPolicy: "none" or null indicates that AKS network policy enforcement is not enabled. In that state, pod-to-pod traffic is not being controlled by a network policy engine. • networkPolicy: "azure" indicates Azure Network Policy Manager is configured. This is still a valid setting today, but Microsoft has published a retirement date of September 30, 2028 for Azure NPM on Linux nodes, so this should usually be treated as a transitional state rather than the preferred long- term target. • networkPolicy: "calico" indicates Calico is configured as the policy engine. This is a supported AKS option and should be assessed against your approved- engine standard. • networkPolicy: "cilium" together with networkDataplane: "cilium" indicates a Cilium-based AKS configuration, which aligns with Microsoft’s current Azure CNI Powered by Cilium model. Microsoft recommends Cilium for new Linux deployments because of its eBPF-based enforcement and broader feature set. • networkPlugin and networkPluginMode should also be reviewed because engine support depends on the broader AKS networking model. For example, Microsoft documents Azure CNI Powered by Cilium using Azure CNI with networkDataplane: cilium, and the managed cluster schema shows these fields are part of the same evaluated network profile. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Use HTTPS with valid TLS certificates for externally exposed workloads
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This helps protect externally exposed AKS applications by ensuring client connections use HTTPS instead of plaintext HTTP at the cluster entry point. In AKS, that protection is typically applied at the ingress or gateway layer, where external web traffic is accepted and routed to backend services. Using TLS at that layer reduces the risk of exposing application traffic, credentials, session data, or other sensitive content in transit.
Rationale: In AKS, external HTTP-like traffic is normally terminated by an Ingress controller or Gateway implementation, not by the layer-4 Standard Load Balancer itself. That means the relevant enforcement point for this control is the layer-7 listener that accepts requests for the application hostname. When that listener is configured for HTTPS, the client performs a TLS handshake with the endpoint, validates the server certificate for the requested DNS name, and establishes an encrypted session before any HTTP payload is exchanged. AKS supports this model through ingress configurations that bind a certificate to the tls section of an Ingress resource, including certificate material sourced from Azure Key Vault and referenced through the generated Kubernetes TLS secret. The ingress path can then perform TLS termination and forward traffic to backend services according to the configured routing rules.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: Remediate by ensuring every externally exposed AKS web entry point is published through an Ingress or Gateway listener configured for HTTPS/TLS, with a valid certificate bound to the public hostname. In AKS, HTTPS protection is typically implemented at the layer 7 ingress or gateway layer, where client traffic is accepted and TLS is terminated before traffic is forwarded to backend services. The remediation objective is to eliminate plaintext HTTP exposure for public application endpoints and standardize certificate-backed TLS for all external web traffic. 1. Update each public Ingress or Gateway that currently exposes HTTP-only traffic so the listener uses HTTPS or TLS for the published hostname. In AKS, ingress is the supported control point for external HTTP-like traffic and SSL/TLS termination. 2. Bind a valid certificate and private key to each exposed hostname, either through a Kubernetes kubernetes.io/tls secret or through an AKS-supported certificate integration such as Azure Key Vault. 3. Ensure the certificate subject or SAN matches the DNS name being published so the listener can complete TLS negotiation correctly for the requested host. AKS application routing guidance is based on configuring certificates for the custom domain used by the ingress endpoint. 4. Where the cluster uses the application routing add-on, standardize certificate management through the supported Key Vault-backed pattern so TLS material is centrally managed and available to the ingress path. 5. After remediation, verify that public endpoints redirect or serve over HTTPS only, that the listener presents the expected certificate, and that backend routing still Internal Only - General functions after TLS termination. AKS ingress supports SSL/TLS termination as part of the application entry configuration.

check.check-content: Its important to review this at the Ingress or Gateway layer, since in AKS those components are the primary enforcement points for external HTTP and TLS termination. The purpose of the review is to confirm that public application entry points are not exposing client traffic over plaintext HTTP and that every externally published hostname is protected by a certificate-backed HTTPS or TLS listener. In AKS, ingress can provide SSL termination, and the application routing add-on supports certificate-based HTTPS using Azure Key Vault–integrated patterns. Internal Only - General • Review all externally exposed Ingress and Gateway resources and identify every public hostname, listener, and route used to publish HTTP-like application traffic. In AKS, these are the resources where external traffic handling is defined. • For each exposed hostname, verify the listener is configured for HTTPS or TLS rather than HTTP-only exposure, and confirm the configuration includes a valid certificate reference for termination. AKS Gateway and ingress configurations are the enforcement points for this control. • Confirm the certificate source is valid and intentional, such as a Kubernetes TLS secret or a certificate synchronized from Azure Key Vault, and verify the certificate is bound to the correct hostname. AKS application routing supports SSL/TLS certificate use through these patterns. • Treat externally exposed HTTP-only listeners, missing TLS secret references, or public hostnames without certificate-backed listener configuration as findings, because those conditions indicate traffic can reach the workload entry point without HTTPS protection. • If the cluster uses the application routing add-on, also verify the intended certificate-management path is in place, since managed NGINX ingress supports secure HTTPS exposure and Key Vault-backed certificate integration for AKS- hosted applications.

Rule.title: Manage Kubernetes RBAC users and groups with Microsoft Entra ID
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using Microsoft Entra ID for AKS user access helps ensure that Kubernetes permissions are tied to centrally managed enterprise identities and groups instead of disconnected, cluster-local user handling. At a high level, this improves control over who can authenticate to the cluster and lets access decisions follow the organization’s normal identity lifecycle, such as user onboarding, group membership changes, and access removal.
Rationale: In AKS, Microsoft Entra integration supplies the authentication layer for Kubernetes access through an OpenID Connect-based flow, and AKS-managed integration now handles the application plumbing that older legacy integrations required administrators to register manually. After the user authenticates, Kubernetes RBAC evaluates that Entra user or group identity through RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects inside the cluster. For user access, newer AKS clusters use the exec credential format with kubelogin, which acts as the client-go credential plugin for Microsoft Entra authentication. This lets AKS use enterprise identities for Kubernetes authorization decisions without maintaining separate Kubernetes user accounts in the cluster itself.</VulnDiscussion>

Where the goal is to ensure all human access is Entra- governed, also disable local accounts so static local admin credentials don’t remain available as a parallel access method; AKS guidance notes that if local accounts are disabled on an existing cluster, cluster certificates should be rotated to revoke previously issued local-account credentials.

check.check-content: Review the AKS cluster configuration to confirm user authentication is integrated with Microsoft Entra ID and that cluster authorization is being managed through Kubernetes RBAC bindings for Entra users or groups, rather than relying on local cluster credentials. A brief audit should verify that AKS-managed Entra integration is enabled, that appropriate Entra admin group object IDs are configured, and that local accounts are disabled where the security standard requires removal of the alternate --admin access path. AKS documents Entra-integrated Kubernetes RBAC as a supported model, and separately documents disabling local accounts to prevent non-auditable admin credential use. Internal Only - General

Rule.title: Use Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Using Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization helps centralize AKS access control in the same Azure IAM model used for other Azure resources, instead of managing human-user permissions only through in-cluster Kubernetes bindings. At a high level, this improves consistency, makes access assignment easier to govern across subscriptions and clusters, and supports least-privilege access by assigning only the Azure roles needed for Kubernetes API use.
Rationale: In AKS, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization uses a Kubernetes authorization webhook after the user is authenticated through Microsoft Entra ID. Requests to the Kubernetes API follow the Entra-integrated authentication flow, and once the calling identity is validated, AKS uses Azure RBAC role assignments to determine what Kubernetes resources that identity can access. AKS supports this model with built-in Azure roles such as Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader, Writer, Admin, and Cluster Admin, and it also allows the use of custom Azure roles where needed. This authorization model depends on managed Microsoft Entra integration being enabled on the cluster first. It also requires the Microsoft Entra tenant used for authentication to be the same tenant associated with the subscription that contains the AKS cluster. Identities that do not authenticate through Entra, such as Kubernetes service accounts, are not evaluated through Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization and continue to use standard Kubernetes RBAC instead. When custom Azure RBAC roles are used, permission design should account for the difference between custom resource definitions (CRDs) and standard Kubernetes resources. CRD read access is typically handled with a broader managed cluster read permission, while standard Kubernetes objects can usually be authorized with more granular API-group-specific actions. This helps keep custom roles functional while still applying least-privilege scoping where finer control is supported.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.fixtext: If the cluster is not using Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, enable AKS- managed Microsoft Entra integration first, then enable Azure RBAC on the cluster and move user access management to Azure role assignments using the built-in AKS Kubernetes RBAC roles or approved custom roles. For stronger control, pair this with disabling local accounts so static --admin access does not remain available as an alternate path; if local accounts are disabled on an existing cluster, rotate cluster certificates to revoke previously issued local-account credentials. Also review any custom role design for CRD coverage, because CRD reads require broader managed- cluster read scope than standard Kubernetes objects.

check.check-content: Review the AKS cluster to confirm AKS-managed Microsoft Entra integration is enabled and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization is turned on, because Azure RBAC for Kubernetes depends on managed Entra integration first. Then verify that access for human users and groups is being granted through Azure role assignments for Kubernetes authorization rather than primarily through in-cluster RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects for those Entra identities. As part of the review, confirm the cluster is using the same Entra tenant as the subscription that contains the AKS cluster, since that is a requirement for this authorization model.
